The study, conducted by researchers Anusha M. Sharma, Sachin David, Parasmal Suresh, Sivadas Swathi Krishna, Neethu Puthalon Kunnath, Beena Karimbuvayalil Vasudevan, Lalitha Biswas, and Keechilat Pavithran, evaluated 358 women residing in underserved localities of the Idukki district. Among the screened cohort, real-time polymerase chain reaction assays and subsequent genetic sequencing identified high-risk human papillomavirus in 2.23 percent of participants, corresponding to eight positive individuals. Notably, while the established carcinogenic type HPV16 accounted for a portion of the positive findings, the researchers observed a notable variety of non-vaccine high-risk genotypes, uncovering localized viral profiles that provide foundational baseline data for regional public health evaluations and future preventive strategies. Cervical cancer represents a substantial global public health challenge, ranking as the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, with approximately 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths recorded in 2022. Nearly 94 percent of these fatal outcomes occur within low- and middle-income nations, underscoring pronounced international disparities regarding access to early screening programs, diagnostic interventions, and prophylactic vaccination. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus constitutes the established primary etiological driver of cervical malignant neoplasms. In India, cervical malignancy is the second most common cancer among women, responsible for an estimated 127,526 new diagnoses and 79,906 deaths annually according to GLOBOCAN 2022 statistics. The nationwide burden accounts for 6 to 29 percent of all female cancers, accompanied by striking regional variations and elevated disease incidence across rural territories where healthcare infrastructure and routine screening remain severely constrained. Epidemiological assessments indicate that annual cervical cancer incidence rates across India fluctuate markedly between 4.9 and 27.7 cases per 100,000 women, with particularly heightened burdens observed in northeastern areas as well as parts of southern and central regions. Infection rates in the general female population similarly exhibit wide geographic heterogeneity, spanning from approximately 10 percent in specific western and southern locales to upwards of 60 percent across sections of eastern India. Although multi-centre national investigations have documented that HPV16 and HPV18 together account for 74 to 78 percent of cervical cancer cases throughout India, other oncogenic viral types such as HPV33, HPV35, HPV45, and HPV58 contribute significantly depending on the local geographical context. In an earlier community assessment conducted on Vypeen Island in Kerala, researchers documented a 2 percent high-risk human papillomavirus prevalence characterized predominantly by HPV16 and HPV33, emphasizing the necessity of gathering targeted surveillance data from isolated settlements. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding To address persistent knowledge gaps concerning viral circulation in remote regions, the research team organized institutional outreach screening camps across six rural and tribal villages within Kerala’s Idukki district: Kumily, Vandiperiyar, Marayoor, Devikulam, Mankulam, and Kanthalloor. These hospital-led initiatives were specifically structured to provide free cervical cancer screening and clinical counselling to underserved demographics lacking routine medical services. A total of 358 voluntary participants aged 30 years and older were enrolled, encompassing both asymptomatic individuals and symptomatic attendees seeking general health examinations. Demographic characterization revealed that women aged 35 to 45 years and 45 to 55 years constituted 70 percent of the total enrolled cohort. Cervical cellular specimens were collected by trained healthcare practitioners utilizing specialized brushes and EziPrep collection vials, followed by immediate cold storage at 4 degrees Celsius and prompt transfer to laboratory freezers maintained at minus 20 degrees Celsius. Genomic deoxyribonucleic acid was isolated from the preserved cervical samples within three to five days of collection using commercial QIAamp extraction kits. Initial molecular screening was performed using the QIAscreen real-time PCR assay on a Rotorgene Q system, which evaluates high-risk viral activity by targeting the conserved E7 gene across 15 high-risk genotypes, including HPV16, HPV18, HPV31, HPV33, HPV35, HPV39, HPV45, HPV51, HPV52, HPV56, HPV58, HPV59, HPV66, HPV67, and HPV68. The diagnostic workflow utilized multiplex four-reporter fluorophores, simultaneously tracking human beta-globin internal control integrity, HPV16, HPV18, and a composite pool of the 13 remaining high-risk strains. Cycle quantification thresholds verified sample validity and viral presence, establishing positive diagnostic cutoffs below 36 cycles for types 16 and 18, and below 33.5 cycles for the pooled hrHPV channel, alongside strict beta-globin verification requirements. Discover more Donate to Research Find Conferences Health Among the 358 screened individuals, eight specimens produced positive real-time PCR outcomes for high-risk human papillomavirus, establishing an overall prevalence of 2.23 percent with an exact Clopper-Pearson 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.97 percent to 4.34 percent. Within these eight detected cases, two infections were identified specifically as HPV16 through genotype-specific real-time PCR amplification. Notably, HPV18 was not detected in any participant throughout the study population. The remaining six positive cervical specimens fell into the pooled high-risk category and required comprehensive Sanger sequencing for definitive genotype resolution. To achieve precise strain characterization, researchers amplified a 450-base-pair segment of the viral L1 structural gene using consensus degenerate primers MY09 and MY11. Sequence alignment via BLAST interrogation against reference databases identified the presence of HPV31, two distinct occurrences of HPV35, HPV45, HPV66, and HPV70, demonstrating that non-vaccine strains predominated among the positive findings. Phylogenetic reconstructions grounded in the sequenced partial L1 gene regions confirmed the evolutionary relationships between the Kerala viral isolates and globally circulating human papillomavirus lineages. Using the maximum likelihood estimation method combined with the Kimura two-parameter substitution model and 100 bootstrap replicates in MEGA version 11 software, the investigators demonstrated that the recovered isolates clustered closely with verified international reference strains, indicating high genetic sequence conservation rather than novel divergence. The Kerala HPV31 and HPV35 isolates clustered alongside reference strains reported from the United States, China, Brazil, and Luxembourg with 97 percent and 99 percent bootstrap support. The HPV45 isolate grouped with counterparts from China and Luxembourg at 96 percent bootstrap confidence, while HPV66 showed 100 percent alignment with globally distributed reference sequences, and HPV70 resolved into a clade containing Brazilian, Togolese, and Chinese strains with 85 percent bootstrap support. The identification of HPV66 and HPV70 in this rural Kerala cohort is of particular epidemiological interest because neither genotype is targeted by existing bivalent, quadrivalent, or nonavalent prophylactic vaccines. While bivalent formulations cover HPV16 and HPV18, and nonavalent immunizations protect against seven oncogenic variants including types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58, they exclude HPV66 and HPV70 entirely. HPV66 is classified as a possibly carcinogenic agent with documented involvement in cervical lesions, for which cross-protective immunity remains doubtful. HPV70, traditionally categorized as a probable high-risk strain, has increasingly been detected in high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive squamous cell carcinoma, presenting negligible likelihood of vaccine cross-protection due to its phylogenetic divergence from vaccine-included strains. Furthermore, although HPV35 has recognized oncogenic associations, it is not directly formulated into current vaccines, and documented cross-protection conferred by bivalent vaccines remains incomplete and waning over time. The detection of HPV45 in an HIV-negative rural Indian population also carries notable epidemiological significance, given that this recognized oncogenic genotype is more frequently documented as a predominant driver of cervical malignancy in sub-Saharan African settings. While HPV45 is incorporated within modern multivalent prophylactic vaccine formulations, its observed occurrence in southern India underscores the necessity of continuous molecular surveillance to observe how localized viral distributions align with immunization policies over time. The overall 2.23 percent prevalence observed in Idukki closely matches the 2 percent infection rate identified in the team’s prior community assessment on Vypeen Island, contrasting sharply with hospital-based Indian investigations from Bihar and Andhra Pradesh that report prevalence figures between 37.3 percent and 86.7 percent due to the inclusion of symptomatic patients and individuals presenting with active cervical lesions. The study authors acknowledged several important methodological limitations inherent to the investigation’s cross-sectional framework. The total sample cohort was limited to 358 voluntary participants across six rural villages, which restricts the direct generalizability of the epidemiological findings to the broader female population of Kerala or other diverse territories across India. The single-timepoint cross-sectional sampling captures only a momentary snapshot of viral presence and genotype distribution, precluding longitudinal evaluation of infection clearance, viral persistence, or clinical progression toward precancerous cervical intraepithelial lesions. Furthermore, recruitment through voluntary community medical camps carries inherent selection bias, as attendees may possess differing health-seeking motivations compared to the non-screened population. Finally, Sanger sequencing of consensus L1 amplicons preferentially amplifies dominant viral strains, meaning underlying minor co-infections cannot be entirely ruled out despite no mixed profiles being identified. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the investigation identified HPV52 and HPV58 as the most frequently detected genotypes across the cohort. Furthermore, among participants carrying an International Agency for Research on Cancer Group 1 carcinogenic genotype, nearly four in five women harbored neither HPV16 nor HPV18. The investigation addressed an important information gap in southern Vietnam, where community-based HPV genotype data remain limited. In this part of the Mekong Delta, local screening programmes face the practical challenge of interpreting genotype-specific risk in a population with low documented HPV vaccination. To provide empirical evidence for this setting, the researchers described overall HPV prevalence, the distribution of carcinogenic genotypes designated as Group 1 by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, infection multiplicity, woman-level detection of HPV16 and HPV18, and woman-level detection of at least one genotype included in the nonavalent vaccine. Fieldwork was conducted between January and June 2026 across Ca Mau Province. The research team utilized a three-stage sampling design with random selection procedures to recruit ever-married women between the ages of 25 and 65 years. From an eligible response-rate denominator of 1,565 women, a total of 1,193 women enrolled in the study, yielding a response rate of 76.2 percent. Because stage-specific selection probabilities were unavailable from the sampling process, the researchers reported all prevalence estimates as unweighted descriptive proportions for the enrolled cohort. Discover more Book a Checkup Check Symptoms View Census Data Get Health Tips Cancer Cervical specimens obtained from the enrolled participants were tested for 23 distinct HPV genotypes using real-time polymerase chain reaction methods. Cervical cytology was performed concurrently alongside the molecular diagnostic testing. To convey the precision of their findings, the authors presented crude proportions accompanied by Wilson 95 percent confidence intervals calculated under the assumption of simple random sampling. In accordance with the descriptive scope of the study, the investigators did not perform inferential statistical comparisons among subgroups or genotype categories. The crude, unweighted HPV prevalence across the sample was 7.1 percent, representing 85 positive women out of the 1,193 enrolled participants, with a Wilson 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 5.8 percent to 8.7 percent. The authors characterized this overall prevalence as low. All 85 women with positive results had a retrievable genotype result. Within this positive group, 78 women, or 91.8 percent, carried at least one high-risk genotype as designated by the assay manufacturer. Furthermore, 66 of the HPV-positive women, corresponding to 77.6 percent, carried a carcinogenic genotype classified under Group 1 by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. In the genotype-specific analysis, HPV52 and HPV58 were the most frequently detected viral strains in the community sample. HPV52 was detected in 20 of the 85 HPV-positive women (23.5 percent), while HPV58 was identified in 14 women (16.5 percent). These were followed by HPV16, HPV51, and HPV59, each detected in 10 of the 85 positive women, representing 11.8 percent for each respective type. Genotype HPV18 was detected in 4 women, accounting for 4.7 percent. In keeping with the study’s protocol, genotype frequencies were not compared statistically. Additionally, multiple genotypes were detected in 25 of the 85 HPV-positive women, establishing an infection multiplicity of 29.4 percent. The study observed notable findings regarding carcinogenic types and vaccine-targeted genotypes. Among the 66 women confirmed to carry an IARC Group 1 carcinogenic genotype, 52 women, or 78.8 percent, carried neither HPV16 nor HPV18, meaning that nearly four in five women with an IARC Group 1 infection had types other than HPV16 or HPV18. When evaluating detection against current immunization targets, at least one genotype included in the nonavalent HPV vaccine was detected in 50 of the 85 HPV-positive women, corresponding to 58.8 percent of those infected. Discover more cancer Find Cancer Care Rent Watercraft Buy Maps Learn Tagalog The investigators articulated explicit limitations regarding the scope and application of these findings. Because stage-specific selection probabilities were unavailable from the field implementation, the reported figures remain unweighted descriptive estimates for the enrolled study sample rather than design-based estimates for Ca Mau Province. While these observations provide a factual description of baseline genotype distribution in a population with low documented HPV vaccination, the authors stressed that genotype frequency alone should not be translated into local triage policy without longitudinal evidence linking individual viral types to histologically confirmed precancer and cancer. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health High-Risk HPV Affects 43 Percent of Screened Women in Mzuzu, Malawi by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 High-Risk HPV Affects 43 Percent of Screened Women in Mzuzu, Malawi Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A cross-sectional retrospective study of women attending gynecological services at Mzuzu Urban Health Centre in Malawi has documented an overall high-risk human papillomavirus prevalence of 42.9 percent. Researchers Cynthia Sifenjane Phiri and Pizga Kumwenda reviewed clinical records from May 2021 to December 2022 to examine viral distribution among local patients. The investigation evaluated how viral presence intersected with demographic factors and health indicators in Mzuzu City, identifying a substantial burden of high-risk infections within the urban clinical cohort. Human papillomavirus infection is the primary cause of cervical cancer, which remains a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Malawi. Because cervical malignancies present severe risks to women across the country, establishing the local distribution of circulating viral types and associated risk factors is essential for optimising screening and vaccination strategies. The study evaluated these clinical dynamics by examining the specific type categories circulating among women seeking gynecological care in Mzuzu. The research team conducted a retrospective cross-sectional review involving 385 women who accessed gynecological care at Mzuzu Urban Health Centre over the twenty-month study timeframe. The investigators reviewed patient clinical records to gather data on age, residential location, and human immunodeficiency virus status alongside diagnostic laboratory results. By compiling these standardized clinical variables across the patient sample, the authors utilized descriptive statistics to assess the overall prevalence of high-risk viral infection and determine genotype patterns. Discover more Buy Maps Book Local Tours Check Symptoms Book a Checkup infections Viral DNA detection and genotyping were performed using the Xpert HPV assay. This diagnostic system identifies HPV 16 and HPV 18/45 individually while detecting a pooled group of eleven other high-risk genotypes. Utilizing this molecular testing platform allowed the researchers to detect critical oncogenic strains while tracking the broader distribution of high-risk infections that fall into the pooled category under the assay protocol. Genotype results showed that the pooled group of eleven other high-risk types predominated, appearing in 34 percent of screened women. In comparison, HPV 18/45 was detected in 11.7 percent of the cohort, while HPV 16 was identified in 9.1 percent. Multiple concurrent infections were documented in 26.7 percent of positive cases, with the most common combination consisting of HPV 18/45 alongside the pooled group of other high-risk types. The study observed notable differences in infection rates across age groups and residential locations. The highest infection rate occurred among women younger than 26 years, reaching 55.6 percent. Geographically, Mzuzu South recorded the largest share of viral cases, accounting for 49.2 percent of all positive results. These findings highlighted a high viral frequency among younger women and a substantial concentration in specific urban residential areas. Viral presence was also notably higher among women living with human immunodeficiency virus. High-risk human papillomavirus occurred in 51.6 percent of HIV-positive participants compared to 40 percent among HIV-negative women. This distribution demonstrated a clear clinical association between HIV status and high-risk viral detection within the outpatient population, emphasizing the heightened vulnerability observed among immunocompromised individuals attending the healthcare facility. Integrating screening into HIV care and prioritizing interventions for younger women may substantially reduce Malawi’s cervical cancer burden. Researchers sought to clarify the inconsistent associations previously reported in global literature regarding HPV involvement in these conditions, particularly given the varying prevalence rates observed across diverse geographic regions. The investigation included a cohort of 113 participants, categorized into three distinct groups: 42 patients with OLP, 31 patients with OSCC, and 40 healthy control subjects who displayed normal oral mucosa. This comparative structure allowed the research team to evaluate how the presence of specific viral genotypes correlated with different pathological states of the oral tissue. To determine the presence and identity of viral DNA within the oral environment, the researchers performed meticulous collection of epithelial cells from the respective lesions and healthy mucosa. The detection and genotyping process utilized a nested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay, a technique chosen for its high sensitivity in identifying low levels of viral genetic material. The analysis classified the detected human papillomavirus genotypes into three primary categories: HPV16, HPV18, and a broader group encompassing other high-risk and low-risk genotypes, referred to as non-HPV16/18 types. This methodological approach enabled a granular view of the viral landscape present in the oral cavity of the study participants, providing a foundation for statistical analysis. The study results revealed varying degrees of HPV DNA detection across the examined groups. Any form of HPV DNA was identified in 25.0% of the healthy control group, 4.8% of the OLP group, and 29.0% of the OSCC group. When focusing specifically on the high-risk HPV16/18 genotypes, the researchers observed prevalence rates of 0% in healthy controls, 2.4% in the OLP group, and 12.9% in the OSCC group. Notably, the presence of HPV16 was detected exclusively within the cohort of patients diagnosed with oral squamous cell carcinoma, suggesting a specific, albeit limited, link between this high-risk strain and malignant oral disease within this particular study population. Discover more Book a Checkup View Census Data Get Health Tips Read Med Journals Find Cancer Care Statistical comparison between the OSCC group and the healthy control group indicated no statistically significant difference in the overall prevalence of any HPV DNA, with an odds ratio of 1.23 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.43 to 3.53. This finding suggests that, in this specific population, the mere presence of any HPV DNA was not a standalone marker for increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma. However, when the analysis was restricted to the high-risk HPV16/18 genotypes, the researchers observed a significantly higher prevalence in the OSCC group compared to the healthy controls, with a p-value of 0.032 for the difference between the 4 out of 31 positive OSCC cases and 0 out of 40 positive healthy controls. The findings regarding the oral lichen planus group presented a distinct contrast. Patients with OLP demonstrated a significantly lower prevalence of any HPV DNA compared to the healthy control group, with an odds ratio of 0.15 and a p-value of 0.012. Furthermore, when compared directly to the OSCC group, the OLP participants showed a significantly lower likelihood of carrying HPV DNA, evidenced by an odds ratio of 8.18 and a p-value of 0.007. These observations highlight the complex and potentially protective or exclusionary interactions that may exist between the oral environment in OLP and the persistence or detection of HPV DNA. To ensure the robustness of these findings, the research team conducted logistic regression analyses, which were adjusted for the variables of age and sex. These adjustments were intended to isolate the relationship between HPV positivity and the different clinical groups from potential confounding factors associated with demographics. The resulting adjusted models indicated that neither age nor sex maintained a statistically significant association with HPV positivity in this study, reinforcing that the observed differences in viral prevalence were primarily driven by the underlying clinical condition of the oral mucosa rather than the demographic characteristics of the participants. Despite the detailed genotyping and statistical comparisons, the researchers acknowledged specific limitations inherent in their investigation. The most prominent constraint was the relatively small sample size, which limits the breadth of interpretation and the ability to extrapolate these findings to broader populations. Consequently, while the study provides important data regarding the prevalence of high-risk HPV genotypes in a Thai cohort, the authors emphasized the need for caution in interpreting these results and suggested that larger, multi-center studies may be necessary to further elucidate the relationship between HPV, oral lichen planus, and oral squamous cell carcinoma. Discover more Book a Dentist oral cancer Oral Cancer cancer Cancer In summary, the study demonstrates that HPV DNA is detectable in normal oral mucosa, oral lichen planus, and oral squamous cell carcinoma, with distinct patterns of prevalence. While high-risk HPV16/18 DNA was identified in a minority of the OSCC cases, its total absence in the healthy oral mucosa of this cohort suggests a potential area for further clinical investigation. The lack of evidence for increased HPV16/18 prevalence in OLP patients serves as a crucial data point for understanding oral potentially malignant disorders in this population, even as the researchers underscore the necessity for future research with larger sample sizes to validate and expand upon these findings. The investigation, published in the journal Infectious Agents and Cancer, examined both clinical and community cohorts to gather baseline evidence on high-risk viral distribution and relevant socio-behavioural characteristics. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus constitutes the primary cause of cervical malignancies, yet precise regional data regarding viral prevalence, specific genotype circulation, and linked demographic factors have historically remained sparse across several areas of India. To evaluate these regional dynamics, the investigation recruited a total of 625 women between the ages of 30 and 60 years across two distinct healthcare delivery settings. Participant enrollment took place through a hospital-based gynaecology outpatient department alongside 11 community screening outreach camps operating within the Central Gujarat region. All 625 participants enrolled in the study underwent concurrent diagnostic evaluations comprising Liquid-Based Cytology and molecular testing via real-time polymerase chain reaction. The researchers conducted descriptive analyses to determine the frequency of high-risk viral infection and map genotype distribution across the cohort, alongside exploratory statistical assessments to examine how measured patient characteristics correlated with laboratory-confirmed viral positivity. Discover more Check Symptoms Book a Checkup Order DNA Kits genotypes Cancer Across the complete study population, molecular testing identified high-risk human papillomavirus infection in 20 of the 625 participating women, yielding the aggregate prevalence figure of 3.2 percent. When evaluated by recruitment source, viral positivity varied between the two examination cohorts: the hospital-based outpatient cohort demonstrated a high-risk prevalence rate of 4.29 percent, whereas the community-based outreach cohort recorded a lower positivity rate of 2.17 percent. Among the 20 women testing positive for high-risk strains, genotype distribution analysis revealed that HPV-18 was the predominant variant, detected in 50.0 percent (10 of 20) of cases. HPV-16 represented the second most common variant, observed in 35.0 percent (7 of 20) of positive specimens, while other high-risk genotypes collectively accounted for the remaining 15.0 percent (3 of 20). The investigators also conducted univariate exploratory analyses using crude odds ratios with 95 percent confidence intervals and Fisher’s exact tests to identify potential associations between participant characteristics and high-risk viral detection. These statistical comparisons indicated that reported tobacco chewing was strongly associated with high-risk viral positivity, presenting a crude odds ratio of 32.85 (95% CI 9.43–114.42; p < 0.001). Furthermore, parity of greater than two children was associated with higher viral detection (OR 3.03, 95% CI 1.18–7.77; p = 0.018), as was an age at marriage below 18 years (OR 3.50, 95% CI 1.33–9.20; p = 0.009) and a reported history of menstrual irregularity (OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.11–7.01; p = 0.012). A notable clinical observation emerged when comparing initial cervical cytology classifications with subsequent histological evaluations among high-risk virus-positive participants who underwent colposcopy-directed biopsy. In the cytology assessments, 90.0 percent of the virus-positive individuals were categorized as having negative or low-grade cellular findings. However, subsequent histopathological examination of biopsy tissue identified cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades II or III (CIN II/III) in 45.0 percent of these cases, while invasive cervical carcinoma was histologically confirmed in 15.0 percent, demonstrating that substantial underlying cervical tissue abnormalities may exist despite unremarkable or low-grade screening cytology. In detailing their conclusions, the authors emphasized that while the findings provide valuable preliminary epidemiological data for Central Gujarat, the results must be interpreted with caution. The study’s cross-sectional design precludes establishing temporal sequences or causal relationships, and the total number of confirmed high-risk viral cases was limited to 20 individuals. Consequently, the research team highlighted the necessity of conducting larger, multicentre investigations across India to validate genotype patterns, rigorously evaluate potential socio-behavioural risk factors, and inform regional cervical cancer screening protocols and public health prevention strategies. High-grade cervical lesions, designated as CIN2+, are critical precursors to cervical cancer. The clinical investigation specifically examined human papillomavirus infection, cervical cytology abnormalities, and vaccination status to determine their association with histopathologically confirmed disease. Conducted in an Iranian colposcopy population, the study reviewed medical records spanning a ten-year period, from January 2014 to January 2024. All 246 female participants had undergone colposcopic evaluation during this timeframe. The authors collected data on patient demographics, including age and marital status, alongside clinical characteristics, cervical cytology, human papillomavirus status, and documented HPV vaccination history. Biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ was defined as histopathologically diagnosed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, grade 3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or invasive cervical cancer. Viral testing utilized the PaxView® Kit to detect human papillomavirus and identify high-risk genotypes. To evaluate factors linked to CIN2+, investigators performed univariable and multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression analyses, reporting adjusted odds ratios and 95 percent confidence intervals. Discover more Find Skin Care Check Symptoms Infection infection Study Biology Of the 246 women analyzed in the retrospective study, 50 patients, or 20.3 percent, were diagnosed with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ lesions, while 196 women were categorized as CIN2−. Among the 50 women with CIN2+, 37 cases, or 74.0 percent, were classified as CIN2, and 10 cases, or 20.0 percent, were CIN3. Adenocarcinoma in situ was identified in 2 women, representing 4.0 percent, and invasive cervical cancer was diagnosed in 1 patient, representing 2.0 percent. The distribution of HPV status and cytological results differed significantly between women with CIN2+ and those without, with both differences yielding p-values of less than 0.001. HPV16/18 infection appeared in 56.0 percent of women with CIN2+ compared to 28.6 percent of those in the CIN2− group. In contrast, HPV-negative results were observed in 18.0 percent of the CIN2+ cohort versus 39.8 percent of CIN2− participants. Cytology showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, or HSIL, was recorded in 38.0 percent of CIN2+ cases compared with 10.7 percent of CIN2− cases. In addition, an absence of HPV vaccination was documented in 42.0 percent of the CIN2+ group versus 16.8 percent of women in the comparison group. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression demonstrated that three key factors were independently associated with biopsy-confirmed CIN2+. HPV16/18 infection yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 3.94, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.70 to 9.74 and a p-value of 0.001. Lack of HPV vaccination was associated with higher odds of CIN2+, showing an adjusted odds ratio of 2.20, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.03 to 4.65 and a p-value of 0.042. Women with HSIL cytology exhibited higher odds of CIN2+ than those with normal cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, designated as NILM, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.84, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.09 to 7.54 and a p-value of 0.031. Age, marital status, and other high-risk HPV genotypes showed no statistically significant independent association with CIN2+. The investigators noted that the observed association between the lack of HPV vaccination and higher odds of CIN2+ requires cautious interpretation by clinicians and researchers. Because vaccination timing relative to initial HPV exposure was not recorded in the retrospective dataset, the finding could reflect unmeasured confounding parameters. Prospective studies examining vaccination timing and pre-vaccination HPV status are required to clarify this relationship. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cervicovaginal Microbiome Stability Strongly Links to Human Papillomavirus Clearance and Lesion Regression Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive systematic review synthesizing twelve longitudinal studies across eleven countries has revealed that the temporal stability of Lactobacillus-dominated microbial communities in the cervicovaginal tract is the most consistent microbiome feature associated with human papillomavirus clearance and the regression of cervical pre-cancerous lesions. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the investigation systematically examined how dynamic shifts across community state types correlate with viral persistence, viral clearance, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia transitions over time. Cervical cancer represents the fourth most common malignancy in women worldwide, responsible for an estimated 660,000 incident cases and 350,000 deaths annually, with a burden falling disproportionately on low- and middle-income regions where screening access is restricted. Although persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic human papillomavirus strains—most notably types 16 and 18, which account for roughly seventy percent of cases—serves as the primary necessary biological driver of cervical malignancy, most women clear viral infections spontaneously within two years via host immune mechanisms. This stark epidemiological difference indicates that critical secondary cofactors, specifically the local cervicovaginal microbiome microenvironment, strongly shape viral clearance, persistence, and subsequent neoplastic transformation. To rigorously examine these dynamics, researchers systematically searched PubMed from inception through September 10, 2024, focusing on cohort designs that evaluated cervicovaginal microbiota using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing or equivalent culture-independent profiling techniques at two or more serial clinical time points alongside human papillomavirus infection or cervical lesion status. Out of 1,430 identified initial records, sixty full-text articles were evaluated, culminating in twelve longitudinal investigations enrolling a cumulative total of 1,663 women across eleven countries that satisfied all methodological inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies, with resulting scores ranging from four to nine. Four studies achieved high methodological quality classifications with scores of seven or greater by establishing well-defined cohorts, clear outcome ascertainment, and controlling for critical clinical confounders; seven studies were deemed moderate quality with scores of five or six, predominantly constrained by limited confounder adjustment; and one investigation received a score of four or below due to unadjusted confounding and inadequate reporting of follow-up protocols. Because clinical and methodological parameters—including cohort demographics, follow-up durations ranging from sixteen weeks to three years, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions, and disparate community classification frameworks—exhibited substantial heterogeneity, quantitative statistical meta-analysis was not feasible. Instead, investigators conducted a structured thematic synthesis focused across three predefined scientific domains: baseline microbial community composition and corresponding clinical outcomes; community state type dynamics, transition trajectories, and temporal stability; and microbiome shifts occurring following surgical or therapeutic intervention for cervical lesions. Primary cohorts originated from diverse geographic jurisdictions, including three studies conducted in the United States, three in China, and individual studies based in the Netherlands, Sweden, South Africa, Costa Rica, the United Kingdom, and Italy. In their analytical syntheses, authors identified that baseline cervicovaginal dominance by Lactobacillus species yielded highly consistent positive evidence for both high-risk human papillomavirus clearance and the clinical regression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia across cohorts. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding Across baseline compositional analyses, cohorts revealed that elevated relative abundance of Lactobacillus crispatus and low overall alpha-diversity correlated with a significantly lower prospective risk of squamous intraepithelial lesion progression among high-risk papillomavirus-positive individuals. In cohorts from the United States, Costa Rica, and South Africa, women presenting with grade 2 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia whose baseline cervicovaginal microenvironment was Lactobacillus-dominated demonstrated significantly higher likelihoods of achieving spontaneous lesion regression at twelve and twenty-four months compared to individuals colonized by depleted communities. Conversely, women exhibiting persistent or incident cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse displayed heightened markers of anaerobic dysbiosis at both baseline and study endpoints relative to persistently negative or transiently infected participants. Specifically, baseline colonization with anaerobic taxa including Gardnerella vaginalis and Prevotella amnii predicted disease progression in Costa Rica, while independent prospective cohorts from China linked genera like Atopobium, Sneathia, and Enterococcus with viral persistence, and Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, and Klebsiella with progressive dysplasia. The evaluation of longitudinal transition patterns demonstrated that Lactobacillus-dominated community state types consistently exhibited superior temporal stability across serial samplings, whereas Lactobacillus-depleted communities underwent markedly elevated transition frequencies. In longitudinal follow-ups of human papillomavirus type 16 infections, individuals experiencing persistent viral carriage and high-grade lesion progression displayed significantly more inter-cluster transitions over eighteen months compared to participants who cleared infection. Critically, divergent transition directionality differentiated clinical trajectories: patients achieving cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 regression predominantly shifted from depleted state IV profiles into Lactobacillus iners-dominated state III communities over time, whereas non-regressing individuals consistently shifted in the opposing direction, moving away from lactobacilli toward highly diverse anaerobic states. Investigations utilizing biweekly self-sampling over sixteen weeks confirmed that communities dominated by Lactobacillus crispatus and Lactobacillus gasseri experienced the fewest transitions, underscoring crispatus dominance as the most durable and stable ecological profile. The review also examined microbial alterations occurring among participants undergoing interventions such as loop electrosurgical excision procedures, cervical excision, interferon therapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy across five treatment-focused investigations. Among women undergoing loop excision, fifty-six percent maintained their community state type between baseline treatment and their six-month clinical visit; among individuals whose profiles shifted, fifty-six percent transited between alternative Lactobacillus-dominant states, twenty-four percent transitioned from depleted states into protective Lactobacillus dominance, and twenty percent progressed toward dysbiosis. In an Italian cohort, Lactobacillus crispatus abundance rose notably following surgical excision in both high-grade lesion groups, escalating from thirty-nine to forty-five percent in grade 2 lesions and more sharply from sixteen to twenty-nine percent in grade 3 lesions. In Chinese cohorts, surgical and interferon interventions frequently spurred transitions from depleted states into Lactobacillus iners profiles, and individuals maintaining community stability following chemoradiotherapy exhibited no cancer recurrence, indicating that intervention typically facilitates an immediate partial ecological restoration. A critical focus of the synthesis centered on the complex and disputed ecological role of Lactobacillus iners, which exhibited divergent clinical correlations across the literature. While cross-sectional epidemiological studies frequently link iners dominance to higher risk of papillomavirus carriage relative to crispatus dominance, longitudinal data synthesized in this review documented that prior Lactobacillus iners dominance frequently preceded papillomavirus clearance and correlated with high community stability after excisional lesion therapy. Ecologically, Lactobacillus iners appears to occupy an intermediate transitional niche: it tolerates variable pH levels and anaerobic fluctuations far better than Lactobacillus crispatus, permitting rapid mucosal recolonization following dysbiotic disruption and serving as a functional stepping-stone toward crispatus restoration. Nevertheless, in immunocompromised cohorts, such as women living with human immunodeficiency virus, iners communities displayed pronounced ecological instability, and laboratory data indicate that iners strains can suppress mucosal defense peptides, emphasizing that its prognostic impact is highly context-dependent and governed by host immune competence and surrounding microbial taxa. Biologically, protective Lactobacillus taxa sustain an acidic cervicovaginal environment below pH 4.5 through lactic acid generation, which suppresses oncogenic human papillomavirus E6 and E7 oncoprotein transcription in laboratory experiments, while bacteriocins and hydrogen peroxide production suppress pathogenic anaerobic colonization. In contrast, dysbiotic bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis synthesize destructive proteases and sialidases that degrade mucosal protective barriers and lower secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor concentrations, fostering an inflammatory cytokine environment marked by elevated interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha that impairs localized immune responses. Furthermore, the relationship between papillomavirus and the cervicovaginal ecosystem appears fundamentally bidirectional: the viral E7 oncoprotein impairs mucosal NF-kappaB and Wnt/beta-catenin pathways, attenuating host antimicrobial peptides essential for lactobacilli persistence. This bidirectional mechanism creates an adverse biological feedback loop wherein microbial dysbiosis promotes viral persistence, which progressively reinforces mucosal dysbiosis and facilitates oncogenic dysplasia. Despite these informative findings, the systematic review highlighted severe methodological limitations across the published literature that constrain conclusive causal determinations. The authors emphasized that their search was restricted solely to PubMed and carried out by a single reviewer, introducing potential study selection biases. Methodological heterogeneity was widespread: included cohorts classified vaginal microbiota using between three and seven community state types, frequently aggregating disparate anaerobic microbiomes into a single generic classification and masking species-level nuances. Additionally, variable 16S sequencing hypervariable regions such as V1-V3, V3-V4, and V4 compromised direct comparisons, while infrequent sampling intervals ranging up to annual visits risked missing rapid intermediate community fluctuations. Most importantly, only two of the twelve investigations formally adjusted for critical confounding variables, including sexual activity, antibiotic administration, ethnicity, hormonal contraception, or concurrent human immunodeficiency virus status, leaving residual behavioral confounding as an alternative explanation for many reported associations. Ultimately, the review emphasizes that current observational evidence does not support the implementation of microbiome-directed interventions, such as commercial probiotics, prebiotics, or vaginal microbiome transplantation, within routine clinical papillomavirus monitoring or dysplasia management. While mechanistic studies demonstrate theoretical biological plausibility for targeted bacterial therapies, robust randomized controlled clinical trials evaluating validated cervical neoplastic outcomes remain entirely absent. The authors conclude that future research must establish harmonized classification frameworks, utilize standardized sampling intervals of three months or shorter, and employ comprehensive shotgun metagenomic sequencing capable of strain-level resolution and functional metabolic pathway analysis. Longitudinal investigations that rigorously control for behavioral determinants and host immunology will be essential to establish whether maintaining a stable, protective cervicovaginal microenvironment can be translated into targeted, evidence-based preventive therapies against cervical malignancy. Laryngeal cancer predominantly affects elderly male individuals with prolonged histories of tobacco and alcohol consumption, making its occurrence in young female individuals exceptionally uncommon. In this newly reported brief report, researchers evaluated a young Han Chinese patient presenting with persistent hoarseness who possessed no history of smoking, alcohol use, or radiation exposure. Comprehensive diagnostic testing revealed the presence of high-risk viral DNA within tumor tissue alongside objective ambulatory evidence of acidic reflux reaching the upper airway, highlighting potential non-traditional pathogenic contributors in atypical head and neck squamous neoplasms. Laryngeal malignancy represents one of the most frequent tumors of the head and neck, displaying sharp epidemiological variations across demographic categories. Disease incidence typically increases markedly after age fifty and reaches peak levels beyond sixty-five years of age, reflecting decades of cumulative exposure to inhaled tobacco smoke and ethanol. Reported male-to-female incidence ratios range between 6.4 to 1 and 24.2 to 1 in established epidemiological literature. Furthermore, anatomical distribution patterns differ between sexes, with supraglottic lesions occurring more frequently in women, followed subsequently by glottic lesions. Given that estrogen declines after menopause have been suggested to alter female biological susceptibility, early-onset glottic carcinoma in young women devoid of classic lifestyle exposures remains an extraordinarily unusual clinical presentation. The patient presented with a primary complaint of persistent hoarseness of insidious onset that had progressively worsened over more than four months beginning in January 2025. She was admitted on April 22, 2025, with an unremarkable medical background that lacked chronic hypertension, diabetes, or earlier viral infections. Physical and historical evaluations confirmed an absence of prior cytotoxic therapy, radiation exposure, or family history of head and neck cancers. Prior to her evaluation at the reporting medical center, an outside laryngoscopic examination in March 2025 identified a left vocal fold mass, leading to an initial supported laryngoscopic resection on April 1. Pathological review of that surgical specimen demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma in situ, prompting referral for specialized intervention to establish clear surgical margins. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding Specialized re-evaluation at the tertiary outpatient clinic confirmed mild congestion across both vocal folds, incomplete glottic closure, and a visible leukomembranous attachment situated at the anterior to middle portion of the left vocal cord while maintaining vocal cord mobility. Review of histological preparations revealed squamous epithelial carcinoma in situ defined by severe dysplasia, papillary growth, mitotic figures, and enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei. Subsequent immunohistochemical profiling showed mottled p16 expression, intact wild-type p53 protein levels, epidermal growth factor receptor scoring of 2+, and a Ki-67 proliferative index reaching approximately thirty percent. Preoperative laryngeal magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated slight focal swelling of the left vocal fold without invasive extension into surrounding soft tissue or cervical lymphadenopathy. To investigate underlying oncogenic alterations, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue samples underwent dedicated virological testing using the Lcn polymerase chain reaction method. The molecular assay yielded positive detection for high-risk HPV18 DNA within the tumor specimen. To determine whether secondary somatic mutations contributed to malignant transformation in the absence of external carcinogens, investigators executed targeted next-generation sequencing across a panel of 535 cancer-related genes. The comprehensive genomic panel detected no actionable somatic driver mutations, no elevation in tumor mutation burden, and no microsatellite instability, indicating that standard genomic driver mechanisms common to smoking-related head and neck cancers were entirely absent in this young non-smoking patient. Discover more Donate to Research Find Conferences health Parallel objective evaluations focused on chemical mucosal injury through twenty-four-hour multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH monitoring. The ambulatory diagnostic study demonstrated pathological laryngopharyngeal reflux, documenting three distinct reflux episodes: one upright acidic air-fluid event, one upright weakly acidic air-fluid event, and one supine acidic air-fluid event. Independent otolaryngologic scoring supported these objective findings, showing a Reflux Finding Score of 10 against a diagnostic threshold of greater than 7, and a patient-reported Reflux Symptom Index of 15 exceeding the threshold of 13. However, her Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Questionnaire score remained low at 3, and her DeMeester score was 7.1, well below the diagnostic cut-off of 14.72 for gastroesophageal reflux disease, while gastroscopic inspection confirmed chronic gastritis. Psychological screening conducted upon hospital admission characterized the patient’s baseline mental well-being alongside her physical symptoms. Standardized inventories revealed mild depressive manifestations, recorded as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score of 5, paired with mild anxiety indicated by a Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 score of 5. The patient also registered an Esophageal Hypervigilance and Anxiety Scale score of 7. Investigators noted that while psychological distress may amplify subjective symptom awareness and perception of reflux episodes, such psychological variables functioned as contextual modifiers for perioperative care rather than direct oncogenic drivers. Following surgical clearance, the surgical team performed trans-supraglottic laryngoscopic laser-assisted anterior commissure partial laryngectomy under general anesthesia on April 27, 2025. Postoperative laryngoscopy demonstrated preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility with localized pseudomembrane development over the operative field and no purulent discharge. Following surgery, the patient entered a standardized management regimen incorporating targeted medical anti-reflux treatment combined with supportive psychological care. At eleven months of clinical follow-up, endoscopic surveillance verified complete absence of tumor recurrence with good reported functional quality of life, accompanied by marked reductions across psychological assessment scores at both one-month and nine-month intervals. The findings offer mechanistic insight into how non-traditional risk factors could collaborate to initiate vocal cord neoplasia. In healthy tissue, the laryngeal and hypopharyngeal mucosa lack endogenous carbonic anhydrase enzymes, leaving surface epithelia without protective bicarbonate generation and highly vulnerable to gastric acid and pepsin. Pepsin maintains enzymatic activity at pH 2.0 and, although deactivated at pH 6.5, reactivates upon re-acidification to disrupt intercellular junctions, downregulate E-cadherin, and upregulate vimentin and beta-catenin. These events stimulate epithelial-mesenchymal transition, mucosal permeability, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-8, IL-1A, and CXCL14, compromising the protective barrier and potentially facilitating human papillomavirus penetration into basal epithelial layers. Despite the informative clinical findings, the authors emphasize critical diagnostic limitations inherent to a single case report. Testing confirmed HPV18 DNA within fixed tissue, but the study did not evaluate transcriptionally active viral oncogenesis via viral E6 or E7 messenger RNA assays or RNA in situ hybridization. Furthermore, immunohistochemistry exhibited mottled p16 expression rather than continuous block-like staining typically observed in transcriptionally driven oropharyngeal lesions. The authors conclude that while human papillomavirus and objective pathological laryngopharyngeal reflux represent compelling non-traditional cofactors warranting selective virological and reflux testing in atypical laryngeal lesions, definitive causal relationships and synergistic interactions require validation through expanded cohort investigations. At the molecular level, high-risk human papillomavirus subtypes such as HPV16 and HPV18 drive transformation through genomic integration and disruption of fundamental cell cycle regulators. Once viral DNA enters the nucleus of vulnerable laryngeal epithelial cells, integration into the host genome can stimulate proto-oncogenes including RAS, EGFR, and Myc. This activation drives the cellular transition from the G1 phase into the S phase, accelerating cellular proliferation and fostering tumorigenesis. Simultaneously, the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 target the pivotal tumor suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein, impairing apoptosis and inducing aberrant proteasome-mediated degradation. Furthermore, viral infection modulates the regulation of survivin, cyclin D1, and telomerase, reinforcing cellular immortality and sustaining neoplastic growth in laryngeal tissue. In parallel, gastric reflux exerts complex molecular effects beyond simple acidic chemical burns. Enzymatically active pepsin penetrates the upper airway mucosa, where it alters intracellular microRNA and messenger RNA expression profiles. These molecular shifts upregulate proto-oncogenes such as Ras while simultaneously suppressing tumor suppressor pathways, including BCL2-related regulatory proteins, promoting dysregulated metabolism and unchecked cellular proliferation. In this patient, twenty-four-hour ambulatory monitoring specifically verified two separate episodes of pharyngeal acid reflux, confirming objective exposure of the vocal fold mucosa to acidic damage. Over time, recurrent exposure to gastric juice and pepsin initiates mucosal metaplasia while degrading barrier integrity, creating an environment that substantially facilitates viral penetration and susceptibility to secondary carcinogenic insults. These dual mechanisms support a model of cooperative pathogenesis, wherein laryngopharyngeal reflux and viral infection act synergistically to induce malignant transformation. Chemical erosion from acidic reflux widens intercellular junctions and elevates mucosal permeability, enabling human papillomavirus particles to access deep epithelial and basal cells where viral DNA can integrate into the host genome. Simultaneously, chronic reflux-induced mucosal inflammation and microenvironmental remodeling impair local immune surveillance, blunting the host immune defense and allowing persistent viral oncoprotein activity to proceed unhindered. This synergy provides a compelling biological explanation for laryngeal carcinogenesis arising in non-smoking young patients whose tumors lack classic tobacco-related genomic alterations. Recognizing these non-traditional etiologies holds direct relevance for clinical evaluation and personalized patient management. In young female patients who develop laryngeal malignancies without traditional tobacco or alcohol exposure, tumor development may be driven by complex interactions involving viral infection, chronic mucosal inflammation, and endocrine hormone profiles. The authors emphasize that routine clinical assessment of clinically atypical laryngeal lesions should incorporate selective virological assays, ideally combining HPV DNA testing with E6 and E7 expression profiling, alongside individualized, stepwise evaluations for occult reflux disease. Such comprehensive diagnostic stratifications could refine prognostic assessments, guide individualized precision therapies, and help prevent disease recurrence in unusual patient populations. Laryngeal malignancy represents one of the most frequent tumors of the head and neck, displaying sharp epidemiological variations across demographic categories. Reported male-to-female incidence ratios range between 6.4 to 1 and 24.2 to 1 in established epidemiological literature. Furthermore, anatomical distribution patterns differ between sexes, with supraglottic lesions occurring more frequently in women, followed subsequently by glottic lesions. Given that estrogen declines after menopause have been suggested to alter female biological susceptibility, early-onset glottic carcinoma in young women devoid of classic lifestyle exposures remains an extraordinarily unusual clinical presentation. The patient presented with a primary complaint of persistent hoarseness of insidious onset that had progressively worsened over more than four months beginning in January 2025. She was admitted on April 22, 2025, with an unremarkable medical background that lacked chronic hypertension, diabetes, or earlier viral infections. Physical and historical evaluations confirmed an absence of prior cytotoxic therapy, radiation exposure, or family history of head and neck cancers. Prior to her evaluation at the reporting medical center, an outside laryngoscopic examination in March 2025 identified a left vocal fold mass, leading to an initial supported laryngoscopic resection on April 1. Pathological review of that surgical specimen demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma in situ, prompting referral for specialized intervention to establish clear surgical margins. Specialized re-evaluation at the tertiary outpatient clinic confirmed mild congestion across both vocal folds, incomplete glottic closure, and a visible leukomembranous attachment situated at the anterior to middle portion of the left vocal cord while maintaining vocal cord mobility. Review of histological preparations revealed squamous epithelial carcinoma in situ defined by severe dysplasia, papillary growth, mitotic figures, and enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei. Subsequent immunohistochemical profiling showed mottled p16 expression, intact wild-type p53 protein levels, epidermal growth factor receptor scoring of 2+, and a Ki-67 proliferative index reaching approximately thirty percent. Preoperative laryngeal magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated slight focal swelling of the left vocal fold without invasive extension into surrounding soft tissue or cervical lymphadenopathy. To investigate underlying oncogenic alterations, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue samples underwent dedicated virological testing using the Lcn polymerase chain reaction method. The molecular assay yielded positive detection for high-risk HPV18 DNA within the tumor specimen. To determine whether secondary somatic mutations contributed to malignant transformation in the absence of external carcinogens, investigators executed targeted next-generation sequencing across a panel of 535 cancer-related genes. The comprehensive genomic panel detected no actionable somatic driver mutations, no elevation in tumor mutation burden, and no microsatellite instability, indicating that standard genomic driver mechanisms common to smoking-related head and neck cancers were entirely absent in this young non-smoking patient. Parallel objective evaluations focused on chemical mucosal injury through twenty-four-hour multichannel intraluminal impedance-pH monitoring. The ambulatory diagnostic study demonstrated pathological laryngopharyngeal reflux, documenting three distinct reflux episodes: one upright acidic air-fluid event, one upright weakly acidic air-fluid event, and one supine acidic air-fluid event. Independent otolaryngologic scoring supported these objective findings, showing a Reflux Finding Score of 10 against a diagnostic threshold of greater than 7, and a patient-reported Reflux Symptom Index of 15 exceeding the threshold of 13. However, her Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Questionnaire score remained low at 3, and her DeMeester score was 7.1, well below the diagnostic cut-off of 14.72 for gastroesophageal reflux disease, while gastroscopic inspection confirmed chronic gastritis. Psychological screening conducted upon hospital admission characterized the patient’s baseline mental well-being alongside her physical symptoms. Standardized inventories revealed mild depressive manifestations, recorded as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score of 5, paired with mild anxiety indicated by a Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 score of 5. The patient also registered an Esophageal Hypervigilance and Anxiety Scale score of 7. Investigators noted that while psychological distress may amplify subjective symptom awareness and perception of reflux episodes, such psychological variables functioned as contextual modifiers for perioperative care rather than direct oncogenic drivers. Following surgical clearance, the surgical team performed trans-supraglottic laryngoscopic laser-assisted anterior commissure partial laryngectomy under general anesthesia on April 27, 2025. Postoperative laryngoscopy demonstrated preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility with localized pseudomembrane development over the operative field and no purulent discharge. Following surgery, the patient entered a standardized management regimen incorporating targeted medical anti-reflux treatment combined with supportive psychological care. At eleven months of clinical follow-up, endoscopic surveillance verified complete absence of tumor recurrence with good reported functional quality of life, accompanied by marked reductions across psychological assessment scores at both one-month and nine-month intervals. The findings offer mechanistic insight into how non-traditional risk factors could collaborate to initiate vocal cord neoplasia. In healthy tissue, the laryngeal and hypopharyngeal mucosa lack endogenous carbonic anhydrase enzymes, leaving surface epithelia without protective bicarbonate generation and highly vulnerable to gastric acid and pepsin. Pepsin maintains enzymatic activity at pH 2.0 and, although deactivated at pH 6.5, reactivates upon re-acidification to disrupt intercellular junctions, downregulate E-cadherin, and upregulate vimentin and beta-catenin. These events stimulate epithelial-mesenchymal transition, mucosal permeability, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-8, IL-1A, and CXCL14, compromising the protective barrier and potentially facilitating human papillomavirus penetration into basal epithelial layers. Despite the informative clinical findings, the authors emphasize critical diagnostic limitations inherent to a single case report. Testing confirmed HPV18 DNA within fixed tissue, but the study did not evaluate transcriptionally active viral oncogenesis via viral E6 or E7 messenger RNA assays or RNA in situ hybridization. Furthermore, immunohistochemistry exhibited mottled p16 expression rather than continuous block-like staining typically observed in transcriptionally driven oropharyngeal lesions. The authors conclude that while human papillomavirus and objective pathological laryngopharyngeal reflux represent compelling non-traditional cofactors warranting selective virological and reflux testing in atypical laryngeal lesions, definitive causal relationships and synergistic interactions require validation through expanded cohort investigations. At the molecular level, high-risk human papillomavirus subtypes such as HPV16 and HPV18 drive transformation through genomic integration and disruption of fundamental cell cycle regulators. Once viral DNA enters the nucleus of vulnerable laryngeal epithelial cells, integration into the host genome can stimulate proto-oncogenes including RAS, EGFR, and Myc. This activation drives the cellular transition from the G1 phase into the S phase, accelerating cellular proliferation and fostering tumorigenesis. Simultaneously, the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 target the pivotal tumor suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein, impairing apoptosis and inducing aberrant proteasome-mediated degradation. Furthermore, viral infection modulates the regulation of survivin, cyclin D1, and telomerase, reinforcing cellular immortality and sustaining neoplastic growth in laryngeal tissue. In parallel, gastric reflux exerts complex molecular effects beyond simple acidic chemical burns. Enzymatically active pepsin penetrates the upper airway mucosa, where it alters intracellular microRNA and messenger RNA expression profiles. These molecular shifts upregulate proto-oncogenes such as Ras while simultaneously suppressing tumor suppressor pathways, including BCL2-related regulatory proteins, promoting dysregulated metabolism and unchecked cellular proliferation. In this patient, twenty-four-hour ambulatory monitoring specifically verified two separate episodes of pharyngeal acid reflux, confirming objective exposure of the vocal fold mucosa to acidic damage. Over time, recurrent exposure to gastric juice and pepsin initiates mucosal metaplasia while degrading barrier integrity, creating an environment that substantially facilitates viral penetration and susceptibility to secondary carcinogenic insults. These dual mechanisms support a model of cooperative pathogenesis, wherein laryngopharyngeal reflux and viral infection act synergistically to induce malignant transformation. Chemical erosion from acidic reflux widens intercellular junctions and elevates mucosal permeability, enabling human papillomavirus particles to access deep epithelial and basal cells where viral DNA can integrate into the host genome. Simultaneously, chronic reflux-induced mucosal inflammation and microenvironmental remodeling impair local immune surveillance, blunting the host immune defense and allowing persistent viral oncoprotein activity to proceed unhindered. This synergy provides a compelling biological explanation for laryngeal carcinogenesis arising in non-smoking young patients whose tumors lack classic tobacco-related genomic alterations. Recognizing these non-traditional etiologies holds direct relevance for clinical evaluation and personalized patient management. In young female patients who develop laryngeal malignancies without traditional tobacco or alcohol exposure, tumor development may be driven by complex interactions involving viral infection, chronic mucosal inflammation, and endocrine hormone profiles. The authors emphasize that routine clinical assessment of clinically atypical laryngeal lesions should incorporate selective virological assays, ideally combining HPV DNA testing with E6 and E7 expression profiling, alongside individualized, stepwise evaluations for occult reflux disease. Such comprehensive diagnostic stratifications could refine prognostic assessments, guide individualized precision therapies, and help prevent disease recurrence in unusual patient populations.
