records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Six-Year Uganda Study Shows High-Risk Non-16/18 HPV Genotypes Dominate Regional Testing by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Six-Year Uganda Study Shows High-Risk Non-16/18 HPV Genotypes Dominate Regional Testing Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A six-year retrospective review of laboratory records at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital in southwestern Uganda has identified an overall high-risk human papillomavirus prevalence of 28.52 percent among tested individuals. Analyzing 4,852 test results compiled between January 2020 and July 2025, investigators observed a gradual upward trend in positive diagnoses across the observation window. The clinical significance of monitoring high-risk viral strains stems directly from their role in disease progression, as persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus causes almost all cervical cancer cases. With global healthcare frameworks steadily moving towards primary testing for cervical cancer screening, understanding regional genotype dynamics has become increasingly important. In this retrospective study, the research team reviewed laboratory records from the regional facility covering a six-year period from January 2020 through July 2025. The investigative protocol gathered detailed data on participant age, district of residence, HIV status, individual test outcomes, detected viral genotypes, and exact dates of testing. All extracted clinical records and multi-year diagnostic datasets were compiled, structured, and statistically analyzed using STATA version 17 software. Analysis of the 4,852 retrieved test records established that diagnostic positivity varied substantially across participant demographics, displaying an inverse relationship with age. The prevalence of high-risk human papillomavirus was highest among the youngest participants aged under 19 years, reaching 66.71 percent based on 12 positive results from 18 tests. Across older cohorts, the measured prevalence of high-risk infections demonstrated a steady and continuous decrease with increasing participant age. Beyond overall positivity, the distribution of identified viral strains revealed that more than half of all positive tests belonged to non-traditional high-risk classifications. Specifically, 65.12 percent of positive results, representing 898 of the 1,379 positive cases, involved non-16/18/45 high-risk genotypes categorized by the investigators as other high-risk HPV. This genotype category also demonstrated a persistent rise over time, climbing from 61.04 percent in 2020 to 63.53 percent in 2025, while also exhibiting a gradual decline with increasing participant age. When examining specific clinical subpopulations, the research team found that participants living with HIV consistently exhibited high rates of these non-16/18/45 genotypes. Within the HIV-positive population evaluated at the referral center, the prevalence of the other high-risk HPV genotype group remained persistently elevated across testing intervals, recording 64.79 percent from 46 of 71 cases in 2020, 66.55 percent from 189 of 284 cases in 2023, and 63.53 percent from 54 of 85 cases in 2025. In their conclusion, the authors noted an elevated overall prevalence of high-risk infections, driven especially by genotypes categorized as other high-risk HPV that inversely correlate with participant age. Based on these observed distributions, the team emphasized the need for implementation of extended high-risk HPV genotyping protocols in regional diagnostic settings. The researchers also highlighted the necessity for further prospective studies to more fully describe individual genotype prevalence, geographic distribution, and longitudinal epidemiological trends. records.content_title: 18岁女孩检出18种HPV亚型阳性,包含10种高危型;医生:极其少见,远期癌变风险显著升高
records.content: 18岁女孩检出18种HPV亚型阳性,包含10种高危型;医生:极其少见,远期癌变风险显著升高 华医网 2026-11-16 05:38发布于北京 问AI · 年轻未生育女性多重感染如何护生育功能? 导 语 什么情况下HPV病毒会导致癌变? 近日,杭州市临平区妇幼保健院妇科接诊了一例极其少见的HPV多重感染病例:年仅18岁的玲玲因外阴持续性疼痛半月余前来就诊,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣,且一次性检出18种HPV亚型阳性,其中高危型多达10种,属于临床极少见的多重混合感染。 玲玲的HPV检验报告/医院供图 接诊医生介绍,玲玲来杭探亲,半个月来外阴隐隐疼痛,总觉得有异物感,最近难受得越来越厉害,正常生活都受影响。专科查体发现其外阴长了典型的菜花状赘生物,从外观来看很像尖锐湿疣。为了查清到底感染了哪些病毒,医生给她做了高精度HPV分型检测,结果让人意外:一共查出18种HPV亚型同时阳性,感染的亚型多、病毒载量很高。 值得高度警惕的是,在18种阳性亚型中,包含10种高危致癌型HPV,是诱发宫颈上皮内病变甚至进展为宫颈癌的核心风险亚型。一次性多重混合感染18种亚型且高危占比极高,提示患者病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂、远期癌变风险显著升高。接诊医生结合玲玲的症状、专科体征及精准HPV分型结果,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣、HPV多重高危感染,目前正在积极治疗中。 医生提醒,尖锐湿疣由人乳头瘤病毒感染所致,多表现为生殖器部位菜花状赘生物,可伴随疼痛、异物感。该患者同时合并多亚型HPV混合感染,尤其是多种高危型持续感染,远期存在宫颈病变风险,需规范治疗并长期随访复查。 那么,如果年轻未生育的女性感染了HPV该怎么办呢?医生介绍:重点要分层评估、避免过度治疗,保护生育功能。大多数生殖道HPV感染依靠自身免疫力,1~2年内自行清除病毒,属于一过性感染,不等于宫颈癌。高危型HPV持续感染才会导致宫颈癌前病变或宫颈癌的发生;单纯HPV阳性、TCT正常≠癌前病变。一般年轻女性HPV感染率高,但病毒清除能力强,所以不要过度恐慌。 建议提高自身免疫力,这对于清除病毒最关键,规律睡眠、减重、均衡饮食,戒烟(吸烟显著降低清除率,增加病变进展风险);适度运动,避免长期熬夜、巨大精神压力等。此外,性生活时建议全程佩戴避孕套,减少交叉反复感染。 如何判断自己是否感染了HPV? 1. 根据症状判断 如果您的皮肤表面出现了不明疣体,有或痛或痒的感觉;或出现非经期出血、同房后出血、白带异常(量多、色黄、有异味)等症状时,建议第一时间到医院做个HPV检查。 2. 无症状时 坚持定期体检,通过HPV联合TCT筛查,可以判断有无HPV感染及宫颈病变。 一项基于美国人群的研究显示,有性行为的男性和女性一生中感染HPV的几率高达80%~90%,而因此患上宫颈癌的女性仅占极小的比例。 人体在感染HPV之后,大多可以通过自身的免疫机制将其清除,所以多数HPV感染是一过性且没有临床症状的,不会产生病变。 什么情况下HPV病毒会导致癌变? 1. HPV病毒持续感染 事实上,导致宫颈癌的主要原因不是感染了HPV,而是无法将其从体内及时清除,使得感染进入了持续阶段。换句话说,HPV持续感染才是宫颈病变发展为宫颈癌的必要条件,而单纯的HPV感染不一定会导致宫颈癌。 从HPV感染发展为宫颈浸润癌可能需要10年、15年甚至20年的时间,经过“HPV感染→持续性HPV感染引起宫颈上皮细胞病变→持续性HPV感染引起宫颈癌前病变→宫颈浸润癌”的四步曲,最终进展为恶性肿瘤。 2. 高危型HPV病毒 是否导致癌变也与感染的HPV型别有关。目前已经发现的HPV有200多种,其中约40种可感染生殖道,根据致癌性的不同分为高危型和低危型。高危型HPV主要有12种,引起宫颈癌前病变II级及以上的几率超过90%,存在致癌风险;低危型HPV主要有11种,主要导致湿疣类病变和宫颈上皮增生,引发宫颈癌的几率不到5%。 从目前的研究数据看,宫颈癌多见于40岁以上女性,从高危型HPV持续感染到宫颈癌前病变,再到发展为宫颈浸润癌,至少需要10~15 年的时间,但约25%的患者会在5年内发展为浸润癌。 日常生活中如何预防HPV病毒感染? HPV虽然主要通过性行为传播,但也可能通过毛巾、便盆、母婴等途径间接传播。预防HPV感染和干预HPV感染后的疾病进程,是HPV感染防治的关键。只有正确认识,规范治疗,才能避免不必要的损伤。 1. 注射HPV疫苗 九价HPV疫苗的预防效果优于四价和二价。目前国内九价HPV疫苗由16~26岁扩龄至9~45岁。在综合考虑价格的前提下,推荐根据适合的年龄段进行选择。 HPV疫苗可以从根本上阻断HPV传播,是特异、有效的预防措施,但对于正在感染相应HPV型别的人群不具有保护作用,因此推荐在高危型HPV感染之前进行接种。 2. 注意私处卫生 养成每天温水清洁阴部的习惯,少穿紧身、不透气的衣物,不给HPV创造藏身之处;性生活前后,男女双方都要用温水清洁外阴部,减少将HPV带入宫颈的机会;同时警惕间接传播方式,如不干净的马桶、宾馆的床单、毛巾等,病毒可以通过皮肤接触,在个人免疫力薄弱时感染。 3. 定期筛查 推荐联合筛查,即在进行HPV病毒筛查的同时,进行宫颈液基薄层细胞学检测(TCT)。如TCT发现异常,推荐进一步阴道镜检查,通过细胞活检取得病理学证据。如阴道镜检查无异常,考虑为慢性宫颈炎。如阴道镜发现异常,可能存在宫颈上皮内瘤变,分为低级别病变和高级别病变。 成年女性建议每2~3年进行一次HPV或TCT筛查,如果是联合筛查,可以间隔3~5年复查一次。 由于HPV疫苗目前尚不能预防所有的高危型HPV病毒,建议有性生活的女性,无论是否接种过疫苗,都应定期进行宫颈癌筛查。 来 源 / 潮新闻、福建省二院健康管理中心

records.content_title: How Mexican Scientist Eva Ramón Gallegos Eliminated HPV in 29 Women
records.content: Eliminating a persistent oncogenic viral infection without cutting, burning, or scarring delicate reproductive tissue represents one of modern gynecological bioengineering’s most sought-after milestones. At Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute, biomedical scientist Dr. Eva Ramón Gallegos spent twenty years refining a non-invasive photodynamic therapy that destroys Human Papillomavirus at the cellular level while sparing healthy tissue. In a landmark Mexico City clinical cohort, her light-activated protocol achieved complete molecular eradication of HPV in one hundred percent of twenty-nine women carrying the virus without premalignant cervical lesions, while clearing infections in nearly two-thirds of patients with precancerous changes. Building on earlier clinical phases across Oaxaca and Veracruz involving more than four hundred women, her work shows how prodrug biochemistry and red-laser physics offer a painless, fertility-sparing defense against cervical cancer. Dr. Eva Ramón Gallegos spent twenty years developing non-invasive cervical photodynamic therapy. Twenty Years of Persistence at Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute Research at ENCB-IPN in Mexico City translated photochemistry into public women’s healthcare. For decades, cervical cancer has ranked among the deadliest malignancies affecting women across Mexico and Latin America, disproportionately striking communities where routine screening arrives late. Even as national screening expanded, millions of women diagnosed with persistent high-risk Human Papillomavirus faced a difficult clinical gap between passive watchful waiting and invasive surgical excision. Working inside the National School of Biological Sciences at the National Polytechnic Institute—known as ENCB-IPN—Dr. Eva Ramón Gallegos set out two decades ago to close that divide using light-activated molecular medicine. Trained in cytopathology, biomedicine, and photodynamic oncology, she studied how photosensitive porphyrin precursors accumulate selectively inside metabolically altered tumor and viral host cells across breast, melanoma, and cervical tissues. Unlike chemotherapy or surgery, photodynamic therapy pairs an inert chemical precursor with harmless visible wavelengths so cellular destruction occurs exclusively where prodrug, light, and oxygen intersect. Sustaining a twenty-year translational program inside a public university demanded steady perseverance across cell-culture assays, optical dosimetry calibration, pathology validation, and multi-state patient follow-up. When IPN reported the Mexico City clinical outcomes in early 2019, the results resonated worldwide by uniting sensitive polymerase chain reaction verification with outpatient accessibility. How High-Risk HPV Oncogenes Drive Cervical Cancer Progression High-risk HPV capsids infect basal cervical keratinocytes and hijack cell-cycle checkpoints. Human Papillomavirus is a non-enveloped, icosahedral double-stranded DNA virus carrying roughly eight thousand base pairs inside a fifty-five-nanometer protein capsid. More than two hundred HPV genotypes exist, yet two high-risk mucosal strains—HPV-16 and HPV-18—cause approximately seventy percent of all invasive cervical carcinomas worldwide. Infection begins when viral particles slip through microscopic mucosal abrasions in the cervical transformation zone to enter dividing basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane. Although healthy immunity clears roughly eighty to ninety percent of transient exposures within two years, persistent high-risk infections unleash two viral oncoproteins—E6 and E7—that dismantle cellular anti-cancer defenses. Viral E6 recruits the host E6AP ubiquitin ligase complex to tag and degrade p53, the master guardian protein normally responsible for halting DNA-damaged cells or initiating apoptosis, while simultaneously activating telomerase reverse transcriptase to immortalize infected clones. Simultaneously, E7 binds and inactivates retinoblastoma protein pRb, releasing E2F transcription factors that force differentiating epithelial cells back into unchecked S-phase DNA replication and progressive chromosomal instability. Because HPV replicates strictly inside intraepithelial keratinocytes without causing viremia or lytic cell rupture, the virus hides subtly from systemic antibodies while gradually integrating its oncogenes into human chromosomes. Over years, persistent E6 and E7 expression drives cervical epithelium through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia stages CIN 1, CIN 2, and CIN 3 toward invasive squamous or glandular carcinoma. Topical 5-ALA and Selective Protoporphyrin IX Accumulation HPV-infected cells convert topical 5-ALA selectively into photoactive protoporphyrin IX. The biochemical cornerstone of Dr. Ramón Gallegos’s protocol is delta-aminolevulinic acid, or 5-ALA, a small naturally occurring amino-ketone that every human cell already uses to synthesize heme for cytochromes and hemoglobin. Rather than injecting systemic synthetic photosensitizers that leave patients sensitive to daylight for weeks, clinicians apply a gentle localized 5-ALA solution topically onto the ectocervix and endocervical canal. Because exogenous 5-ALA bypasses feedback inhibition at the first step of heme synthesis yet remains completely non-toxic in the dark, it diffuses safely across dysplastic and HPV-infected mucosa over a four-hour incubation window. Inside HPV-infected and dysplastic cells, warped Warburg-like metabolic enzyme ratios—elevated cytosolic porphobilinogen deaminase paired with sluggish mitochondrial ferrochelatase—stall final ferrous iron insertion into heme. Because that enzymatic bottleneck blocks heme completion, infected cells trap massive intracellular concentrations of the immediate fluorescent precursor: photoactive protoporphyrin IX, abbreviated PpIX. Healthy surrounding squamous cells and underlying stromal fibroblasts maintain balanced ferrochelatase kinetics, swiftly converting excess PpIX into harmless, non-photosensitive heme. Under diagnostic blue-violet illumination near four hundred five nanometers, PpIX-enriched viral patches emit unmistakable brick-red fluorescence, confirming millimeter-level biochemical selectivity before therapeutic laser exposure begins. 630–635 nm Red Laser Excitation and Singlet Oxygen Physics Non-thermal red laser light excites PpIX to generate short-lived cytotoxic singlet oxygen. Four hours after topical 5-ALA application, when the PpIX concentration ratio between infected keratinocytes and normal stroma peaks, clinicians illuminate the cervix with a calibrated non-thermal red laser tuned to 630 to 635 nanometers. Although PpIX absorbs violet wavelengths strongly at the surface, biophysicists deliberately target its red Q-band absorption peak because 630-to-635-nanometer photons avoid hemoglobin absorption and penetrate several millimeters deep into endocervical crypts where latent HPV resides. Absorbing red photons promotes PpIX into an excited singlet state that undergoes quantum intersystem crossing into a long-lived triplet state, transferring energy via Type II photochemistry directly to dissolved triplet oxygen to generate cytotoxic singlet oxygen (1O2). Because singlet oxygen survives less than a microsecond and diffuses fewer than one hundred nanometers—smaller than a single mitochondrion—oxidative destruction stays locked strictly inside PpIX-loaded HPV host cells through five synergistic mechanisms: Mitochondrial apoptosis induction: Singlet oxygen oxidizes inner mitochondrial lipids where PpIX forms, releasing cytochrome-c to guide HPV-infected keratinocytes into clean programmed apoptosis without inflammatory necrosis. Singlet oxygen oxidizes inner mitochondrial lipids where PpIX forms, releasing cytochrome-c to guide HPV-infected keratinocytes into clean programmed apoptosis without inflammatory necrosis. Direct viral DNA and oncoprotein oxidation: Reactive oxygen species cleave intracellular HPV episomes and denature E6 and E7 oncoproteins across basal epithelial layers. Reactive oxygen species cleave intracellular HPV episomes and denature E6 and E7 oncoproteins across basal epithelial layers. Deep endocervical crypt reach: Coherent 630–635 nm red photons penetrate glandular infoldings several millimeters deep where superficial cautery misses latent virus. Coherent 630–635 nm red photons penetrate glandular infoldings several millimeters deep where superficial cautery misses latent virus. Local dendritic T-cell priming: Apoptotic viral host cells expose viral capsid antigens and damage signals that recruit Langerhans cells and CD8-positive T lymphocytes against residual virus. Apoptotic viral host cells expose viral capsid antigens and damage signals that recruit Langerhans cells and CD8-positive T lymphocytes against residual virus. Concurrent co-pathogen clearance: Cervicovaginal bacteria and fungi rapidly accumulate porphyrins too, clearing co-infections that otherwise fuel chronic mucosal inflammation. Patients remain awake without anesthesia throughout the brief outpatient illumination, feeling at most gentle warmth while laser fluence stays below thermal thresholds. Preserving Cervical Anatomy Without Surgical Scarring Extracellular collagen matrix stays intact so cervical tissue regenerates without surgical scarring. Comparing photodynamic therapy against standard excisional procedures highlights why reproductive specialists and maternal-fetal medicine physicians welcomed ENCB-IPN’s results across Latin America. Conventional loop electrosurgical excision (LEEP) and cold-knife conization save lives whenever high-grade dysplasia nears micro-invasion, yet surgically cutting a wedge-shaped cone of fibromuscular stroma carries documented obstetric trade-offs for younger patients. Removing structural cervical collagen shortens functional cervical length and weakens sphincter integrity, measurably elevating future risks of cervical insufficiency, second-trimester miscarriage, premature membrane rupture, preterm delivery, and endocervical canal stenosis. Thermal cautery and liquid-nitrogen cryotherapy can also leave fibrotic scar tissue that pulls the squamocolumnar transformation zone inward, making subsequent colposcopic surveillance harder to interpret accurately. Post-treatment cytology and colposcopy confirmed healthy epithelial regeneration across treated cohorts. Photodynamic therapy avoids structural tissue loss altogether because acellular type-I and type-III collagen fibers and elastin networks neither synthesize protoporphyrin IX nor denature under non-thermal 630-nanometer illumination. Even microvascular basement membranes beneath the cervical epithelium recover smoothly after transient vasoconstriction, supplying oxygen and growth factors without triggering myofibroblast scar contraction. As apoptotic HPV-infected cells slough away cleanly over several days, intact collagen scaffolds guide healthy basal stem cells to resurface a smooth, unscarred cervix across five structured outpatient steps: Baseline multimodal diagnostic profiling: Every enrolled participant underwent Pap cytology, high-magnification colposcopy, targeted histopathology when lesions appeared, and baseline polymerase chain reaction genotyping to map exact high-risk HPV strains and co-infections. Localized topical 5-ALA prodrug application: Clinicians applied calibrated delta-aminolevulinic acid gel directly over the ectocervix and endocervical canal using a sterile cervical applicator without needles, local anesthetic injections, or surgical clamps. Four-hour selective metabolic conversion window: Patients rested comfortably for roughly four hours while metabolically altered HPV-infected and dysplastic cells converted 5-ALA selectively into brick-red fluorescent protoporphyrin IX. Scheduled 48-hour red-laser photodynamic sessions: Precision optical fiber delivery illuminated the cervical transformation zone and endocervical canal at 630–635 nm across scheduled outpatient visits spaced forty-eight hours apart. Longitudinal cytological and PCR verification: Follow-up evaluations months post-therapy repeated colposcopy, cytology, and sensitive viral DNA amplification to verify both histological tissue normalization and true molecular HPV clearance. Inside the Oaxaca, Veracruz, and Mexico City Clinical Cohorts Fluorescence spectroscopy guided optimal prodrug concentration and 48-hour laser dosing intervals. Rather than relying on a single small pilot group, Dr. Ramón Gallegos systematically refined optical dosimetry and prodrug kinetics across distinct geographic cohorts totaling four hundred forty-nine Mexican women. In the earlier clinical phase conducted across public clinics in Oaxaca and Veracruz, four hundred twenty women received three photodynamic sessions spaced forty-eight hours apart. That initial regimen achieved eighty-five percent complete HPV eradication among lesion-free HPV carriers, eighty-five percent clearance in women presenting with both HPV and premalignant lesions, and forty-two percent resolution in HPV-negative lesions. By tracking cervical surface porphyrin fluorescence before and after each illumination cycle, ENCB-IPN biophysicists discovered that doubling the topical 5-ALA concentration across two forty-eight-hour treatment schemes achieved deeper, more uniform PpIX saturation down to basal stem-cell layers. Painless outpatient delivery made advanced photodynamic care welcoming for Mexico City participants. Testing that doubled-concentration regimen in twenty-nine Mexico City patients delivered the landmark clinical result reported by IPN: one hundred percent HPV elimination in every woman who carried HPV without premalignant lesions. Among Mexico City women who entered the cohort already harboring both HPV infection and premalignant cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, the non-invasive therapy cleared pathology in 64.3 percent of cases, while resolving 57.2 percent of premalignant lesions lacking detectable HPV—with zero collateral injury to healthy vaginal or uterine tissue: Clinical Modality / Cohort Target Patient Group Mechanism of Action Documented Efficacy & Structural Outcome IPN Phase I: Oaxaca & Veracruz (n = 420) Women with HPV and/or premalignant CIN lesions Standard-dose topical 5-ALA + 3 red-laser sessions (48 h apart) 85% HPV clearance (HPV-only & HPV+lesions); zero cervical scarring IPN Phase II: Mexico City Cohort (n = 29) Urban cohort with HPV only, HPV+CIN, or CIN alone Doubled 5-ALA concentration + 2 cycles spaced 48 hours apart 100% clearance in lesion-free HPV carriers; 64.3% in HPV+lesions LEEP / Cold-Knife Conization Persistent high-grade dysplasia (CIN 2 / CIN 3) Electrosurgical wire or scalpel excision of cervical tissue cone 85–95% lesion removal, but shortens cervix and raises preterm birth risk Cervical Cryotherapy / Thermal Ablation Selected low-to-moderate ectocervical lesions Non-selective freezing or heat necrosis of surface mucosa 75–88% ablation; risk of cervical stenosis and missed deep crypt virus Prophylactic HPV Vaccination (L1 VLP) Adolescents & young adults prior to viral exposure Neutralizing antibodies blocking initial viral capsid entry >90% prevention of new HPV-16/18 infections; cannot clear existing HPV PCR Molecular Verification and Co-Pathogen Clearance Polymerase chain reaction assays verified true molecular absence of high-risk HPV DNA. Crucially, ENCB-IPN researchers refused to declare viral eradication based solely on cleaner microscopic Pap smears or visual colposcopy. Because subclinical viral episomes can linger silently inside deep basal keratinocytes long after surface koilocytes disappear, her laboratory paired cytopathology with sensitive polymerase chain reaction amplification targeting conserved L1 and E6/E7 viral sequences. Confirming negative post-treatment PCR assays across one hundred percent of the lesion-free HPV carriers in Mexico City proved that singlet-oxygen photochemistry paired with local Langerhans and cytotoxic T-cell recruitment drove viral genomes below molecular detection thresholds. Parallel microbiological testing across the cohort uncovered an equally practical clinical bonus for women’s reproductive health. Chronic cervicovaginal co-infections damage epithelial tight junctions, deplete protective lactobacilli, and generate nitrosative inflammation that accelerates high-risk HPV DNA integration into host chromosomes. In IPN’s evaluations, topical 5-ALA photodynamic therapy simultaneously cleared 81 percent of concurrent pathogenic bacterial infections—including Chlamydia trachomatis—and 80 percent of Candida albicans fungal infections, restoring balanced mucosal immunity. Complementary Prevention Alongside Global HPV Vaccination Dr. Ramón Gallegos’s laboratory continues training a new generation of Mexican women scientists. Public-health oncologists emphasize that non-invasive photodynamic therapy complements rather than replaces childhood HPV vaccination and routine molecular cervical screening. While prophylactic L1 virus-like particle vaccines remain extraordinarily effective at blocking initial viral entry prior to exposure, vaccine-induced serum antibodies cannot enter basal keratinocytes to clear persistent HPV infections acquired years earlier. For the hundreds of millions of adult women worldwide already living with persistent high-risk HPV—especially in regions where surgical oncology specialists are scarce—an outpatient light-activated therapy bridges the gap between primary vaccination and invasive surgery. Combining vaccination, molecular screening, and non-invasive therapy protects generations of women. Ongoing translational goals for biophotonics researchers in Mexico and abroad include larger multicenter randomized Phase III trials, portable medical LED cervical illuminators suited for rural community clinics, and affordable generic 5-ALA gels. records.content_title: 罕见!年轻女孩同时感染18种HPV亚型|HPV 疫苗:第一针是启动,第二针才筑牢保护!
records.content: 为 近日,杭州临平区妇幼保健院接诊了这一则特殊病例。女孩外阴疼痛就诊,最终确诊外阴尖锐湿疣, HPV检测一次性检出18种亚型阳性,其中包含 10 种高危亚型。接诊医生称该病例十分罕见。 HPV检验报告/医院供图 接诊医生介绍, 女孩 来杭探亲,半个月来外阴隐隐疼痛,总觉得有异物感,最近难受得越来越厉害,正常生活都受影响。专科查体发现其外阴长了典型的菜花状赘生物,从外观来看很像尖锐湿疣。为了查清到底感染了哪些病毒,医生给她做了高精度 HPV分型检测,结果让人意外: 一共查出 18种HPV亚型同时阳性,感染的亚型多、病毒载量很高。 HPV分型检测/医院供图 值得高度警惕的是,在 18种阳性亚型中,包含10种高危致癌型HPV,是诱发宫颈上皮内病变甚至进展为宫颈癌的核心风险亚型。一次性多重混合感染18种亚型 且高危占比极高,提示患者病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂、远期癌变风险显著升高。接诊医生结合女孩的症状、专科体征及精准 HPV分型结果,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣、HPV多重高危感染,目前正在积极治疗中。 展开全文 科普延伸 HPV 也就是人乳头瘤病毒,传播途径不只有 性接触,潮湿公共环境、皮肤微小破损也可能造成间接感染,抓挠还会造成病毒自身扩散 。 HPV亚型众多,低危型多引发各类疣体,包括丝状疣、跖疣、尖锐湿疣等;高危型以16、18型风险最高,持续感染可诱发宫颈癌等肿瘤,早期大多没有症状。 低危型 HPV感染:皮肤或生殖器长疣 低危型 HPV本身没有致癌基因,它引起的多是良性的疣体增生,癌变风险较低。它一般出现在 眼睛周围、手背、前臂 等部位,有米粒至黄豆大小,扁平微微鼓起的小丘疹,数目较多且密集, 颜色起初呈肉或粉色 ,时间久了,还会变成深褐色,会有瘙痒感。 高危型 HPV:早期无声息,后期有肿块 典型代表就是 HPV16型、18型 !致癌性最强,有约 70%的宫颈癌是由这两种HPV病毒引起的,还可能引发外阴癌、肛门癌、口咽癌等多种癌症,还有HPV31型、33型、45型、52型、58型等14种,致癌风险都很高。不过,它们早期通常无症状,到后期才可能出现异常阴道出血、白带异常、局部肿块、小腹坠胀等症状。 定期筛查 +接种疫苗有助降低HPV风险 所以,定期筛查格外重要,建议大家可以去医院做 HPV检测,至少五年一次,还可以做TCT(宫颈脱落细胞学)检查,至少三年一次。 此外,还可以选择接种疫苗,来帮助预防感染 HPV病毒。 去年11月10日起,HPV疫苗正式纳入国家免疫规划,2011年11月10日以后出生、满13周岁的适龄女生有权利和义务免费接种二价HPV疫苗。 HPV疫苗能有效预防子宫颈癌等疾病,为花季少女筑牢青春健康屏障,守护她们的成长。可能有的家长犹豫说:“我的孩子还小,等长大了再打也来得及。”但其实, 初中阶段是接种 HPV疫苗的黄金期:防护效果更好,青春期免疫系统活跃,接种后产生的抗体水平比成年后的水平更高,保护力更强。预防大于一切。17-24岁是我国女性感染HPV病毒的第一个高峰时期,提前接种,能在暴露风险来临前,为孩子筑牢健康屏障。 大家快行动起来,成功预约、按时接种 HPV疫苗。但这里有一个非常普遍的误区: 打上第一针 ≠有完整保护,第一针是免疫启动,第二针才是巩固抗体、拉高保护水平的核心! 同时还要记住两个核心真相: HPV疫苗是预防性疫苗,没有治疗作用。对已经存在的 HPV 感染、已经发生的病变,无法清除;无论二价、四价、九价,只能覆盖对应亚型,疫苗不能替代定期 HPV+TCT 筛查。就算全程打完疫苗,适龄女性依然要按时筛查。 上述罕见的多重 HPV 感染病例,不是制造焦虑,而是提醒我们: HPV的病毒亚型繁多,感染风险真实存在。想防护,优先尽早接种HPV疫苗;约上、打上第一针,只是第一步;按时打卡第二针,完成规范剂次,才能拿到更可靠的保护。 你已经打上 HPV 第一针了吗?记得设置提醒,按时接种下一针!具体接种间隔、剂次,以门诊医生、疫苗说明书为准;如果错过第二针时间,不需要从头重打,尽快前往接种门诊补齐即可。 供 稿 | 马欢欢 初 审 | 马欢欢 复 审 | 王立博 终 审 | 布仁巴图 通辽市疾病预防控制中心 Tongliao Center for Diseases Prevention and Control 关爱健康公卫先行 预防疾病健康通辽 返回搜狐,查看更多

AMCP Nexus 2026| HSES 2026 Advertisement News|Articles|November 20, 2026 For transgender women with HIV, risk awareness and provider trust shape anal cancer follow-up Author(s)Logan Lutton Listen 0:00 / 5:10 Key Takeaways Transgender women experience markedly higher anal cancer prevalence, driven by high-risk anal HPV, with HIV acting as a major cofactor that increases HSIL risk independent of viral suppression or ART use. Consensus guidance recommends screening transgender women with HIV starting at 35 years and without HIV at 45 years, reflecting incidence >70/100,000 person-years in key HIV-affected populations. Follow-through after abnormal cytology is suboptimal; prior data show high referral rates to HRA but less than half completing the procedure, representing a preventable oncologic care gap. Confusion between cytology, HRA, and colonoscopy, plus emotional and physical discomfort, impede adherence; step-by-step explanations and supportive clinician behaviors mitigate distress. Gender-affirming, trusted providers strongly influence uptake, and community support plus HPV-focused education, correct pronoun use, and self-collected sampling could improve completion rates. SHOW MORE Among 16 Black transgender women, 15 with HIV, risk awareness, comfort, provider trust and support shaped whether they completed HRA, according to a new qualitative study. Advertisement Transgender women face an anal cancer prevalence 5.5 times higher than cisgender individuals, a gap the researchers linked largely to high rates of anal high-risk HPV infection. For transgender women living with HIV, knowing that the virus raises their anal cancer risk can push them toward follow-up care, but gaps in screening knowledge, discomfort with the procedure and limited trust in clinicians can still stand in the way, according to the results of a recent qualitative study published in JoVE Journal. The study was led by a team of researchers, including senior author Darren Whitfield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Maryland School of Social Work. Whitfield and his team included semi-structured interviews with 16 Black transgender women who had abnormal anal cytology and were referred for high-resolution anoscopy (HRA), which detects and treats high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), the precursor to anal cancer. Half had completed HRA and half had not. Participants were recruited from a clinic that offers gender-affirming care, and most were 35 or older (81%), stably housed (81%) and living with HIV (94%). How HIV raises anal cancer risk for transgender women Transgender women face an anal cancer prevalence 5.5 times higher than cisgender individuals, a gap the researchers linked largely to high rates of anal high-risk of human papillomavirus (HPV). The authors described HIV as the second most important risk factor in this population. HIV potentiates HPV infection and raises the likelihood of HSIL regardless of viral suppression or antiretroviral therapy use. That overlap matters because HIV is concentrated among transgender women. In CDC’s National HIV Behavioral Surveillance of 1,608 transgender women in seven U.S. cities, 42% received a positive HIV test result. The International Anal Neoplasia Society’s 2024 consensus guidelines recommend that transgender women with HIV begin screening at age 35 and those without HIV at age 45. The earlier start reflects an incidence of more than 70 per 100,000 person-years among transgender women and men who have sex with men with HIV, according to an ASCCP practice advisory. The first U.S. anal cancer screening guidelines for people with HIV followed later that year, according to the National Cancer Institute. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up Follow-through after an abnormal result remains a weak point. In an earlier cohort of 75 transgender women, 49% had abnormal cytology. Of those, 89% were referred to HRA, but only 47% completed it. “This highlights a potential missed opportunity to prevent anal cancer in this population at elevated risk for cancer,” Whitfield and his team wrote in the study. How HIV awareness affects HRA decisions Several participants said knowing their HIV status raised their anal cancer risk factored into their decision. “Being that I’m HIV-positive, that it must be addressed immediately,” said one participant, though she had not completed HRA herself. Still, many could not distinguish anal cytology from HRA or from colonoscopy. Comfort also played a role. Some participants felt emotionally vulnerable having a clinician collect the anal swab, and most who completed HRA reported discomfort that eased when providers explained each step. Provider trust in HIV and gender-affirming care Participants who described positive relationships with clinicians were more willing to follow recommendations. One participant who completed HRA said the specialist her primary care doctor referred her to “made it feel at ease.” Others said they preferred to rely on a physician they already knew, and a lack of affirming communication was cited as a barrier. Whitfield and his team wrote that raising HRA completion may depend on encouragement from providers who serve and are trusted by transgender women. Prior research cited in the paper found an odds ratio of 241.57 for completing anal cytology among transgender individuals when a provider recommended the test. Why HPV gets less attention than HIV among transgender women Participants said anal health is rarely discussed in their community, where HIV has long been the focus. “HIV was the higher thing people was scared to talk about and talk to. It wasn’t about HPV,” said one participant who completed HRA. Others said lacking support kept them away. “If I find out I have something, who do I have to cry to? Nobody,” said one participant who did not complete HRA. The authors recommended gender-neutral HPV education inclusive of transgender women, consistent use of preferred names and pronouns, opportunities for self-collected anal cytology and integration of social support networks into screening programs. They noted the sample came from a single clinic with an existing research partnership and that all participants had healthcare access. Asked what would help more transgender women complete HRA, one participant who did not complete the procedure said providers “should say more caring [things]. Be more compassionate about the things that trans women go through.” Newsletter Get the latest industry news, event updates and more from Managed Healthcare Executive. records.content: Oncologists Urge Adults 45 and Under to Get the HPV Vaccine for Cancer Prevention Modern medicine has made it so that a cancer diagnosis is no longer a death sentence. For instance, survival rates of breast and ovarian cancer have risen, giving us more time to live a life with love. Oncologists are grateful for advances like mammograms to screen for breast cancer, and chemotherapy and radiation to fight the disease. Still, no one would wish a cancer diagnosis on themselves or a loved one. "Treatment still takes a significant physical, emotional and financial toll on patients," Dr. Gabrielle Smith, MD, a gynecologic oncologist with HonorHealth, explains to Parade. "Preventing cancer whenever possible is so important, as it can spare someone that entire experience." She knows we can't control every risk factor for cancer. You may not have had control over a work environment that exposed you to toxic chemicals, for example, and you certainly didn't willingly "sign up" to have certain genetics. Still, as a gynecologic oncologist, Dr. Smith wants people to know all of their options because she doesn't want them to become her patients. Staying up to date or catching up with certain vaccines is one way to lower your risk of certain cancers. "All cancers are diseases of our genes, and sometimes a virus can alter or hijack our genes, which eventually leads to cancer," Dr. Smith says. "When we vaccinate against a known virus that can cause cancer, we have an opportunity to interrupt that process before it starts." Vaccines aren't "just for kids," and flu and COVID-19 shots aren't the only ones available to adults in their 20s, 30s and 40s. For this reason, oncologists urge adults 45 and under to ask about one vaccine in particular, as it could protect them from several cancers. 🩺SIGN UP for Parade's health newsletter with expert-approved tips, healthy eats, exercises, news & more to help you stay healthy & feel your best self💊 Oncologists Are Begging Adults 45 and Under to Ask About This Vaccine Oncologists urge people 45 and under to get the HPV vaccine because it can protect you against six types of cancer: Cervical, oropharyngeal (throat), anal, vulvar, vaginal and penile. The HPV vaccine can stop "the underlying viral infection that causes" these cancers, says Dr. Ami Vaidya, MD, co-chief of the Division of Gynecologic Oncology at the Hackensack Meridian John Theurer Cancer Center. The FDA approved the first HPV vaccine in 2006, and it targeted four variants of human papillomavirus (HPV), a virus that commonly spreads through sexual contact. In 2014, the FDA approved the Gardasil 9 HPV vaccine, which doctors still use today. Dr. Vaidya says it targets nine high-risk viral strains of HPV. Doctors recommend the HPV vaccine to all children ages 11–12 (but children can begin getting the vaccination at age nine). It's a two-dose series for ages 9–14. However, people can receive a three-dose series up to age 45. "The vaccine is made with the outer coating of the virus to teach your immune system to recognize the virus and create antibodies that can then destroy the virus if you are exposed to it in the future, before it causes an infection," Dr. Smith says. "Since the vaccine does not contain any DNA from the virus, you cannot get infected with HPV from the vaccine." Related: 'I'm an Oncologist—This Is the First Symptom I'd Never Ignore in Someone Under 40′ Why Do Oncologists Recommend the HPV Vaccine to People Ages 27-45? The recommended age for the HPV vaccine is 11-12 years, but people can receive their first dose at age 9. Doctors and medical organizations like the CDC continue to recommend the HPV vaccine for people ages 13-26 (the "catch-up" demographic). However, Dr. Vaidya encourages people to ask about the vaccine up to and including age 45, saying the vaccine remains "highly beneficial" for many people. It provides robust protection against any of the nine high-risk viral strains a person has not yet encountered," Dr. Vaidya says. "This is especially crucial for individuals experiencing life transitions—such as re-entering the dating pool after a breakup or divorce—which introduce new opportunities for exposure." She adds that natural HPV infections don't always give you lasting immunity, so the vaccine offers a "much stronger antibody response" that can guard you against reinfection, lower your long-term health risks like throat cancer and protect future partners from transmission. Related: 'I Was Diagnosed With Cancer at 16 and Again at 39—These Were the Very First Symptoms I Noticed' Dr. Vaidya says there's no approved HPV vaccine for people ages 46 and older because many people in this age group were already exposed to the virus during sexual activity. "Immunization can only prevent new infections, not treat or clear existing ones," she says. Dr. Vaidya adds that HPV is a slow-acting virus and usually takes one to three decades of persistent infection to progress to cancer. "A new infection acquired later in life is much less likely to develop into cancer within a person's natural lifespan," she says. But if you're 45 and under, Drs. Vaidya and Smith agree that it's worth asking your doctor about the HPV vaccine. "Health experts recommend 'shared clinical decision-making,' meaning adults should consult with their doctor to determine if vaccination aligns with their current lifestyle and personal risk factors," she says. records.content: Beth Ann Mayer Sun, November 15, 2026 at 5:25 PM UTC 44 (aire images/Getty Images) Modern medicine has made it so that a cancer diagnosis is no longer a death sentence. For instance, survival rates of breast and ovarian cancer have risen, giving us more time to live a life with love. Oncologists are grateful for advances like mammograms to screen for breast cancer , and chemotherapy and radiation to fight the disease. Still, no one would wish a cancer diagnosis on themselves or a loved one. “Treatment still takes a significant physical, emotional and financial toll on patients, ” Dr. Gabrielle Smith, MD , a gynecologic oncologist with HonorHealth, explains to Parade . “Preventing cancer whenever possible is so important, as it can spare someone that entire experience.” She knows we can’t control every risk factor for cancer. You may not have had control over a work environment that exposed you to toxic chemicals, for example, and you certainly didn’t willingly “sign up” to have certain genetics. Still, as a gynecologic oncologist, Dr. Smith wants people to know all of their options because she doesn’t want them to become her patients. Staying up to date or catching up with certain vaccines is one way to lower your risk of certain cancers. “All cancers are diseases of our genes, and sometimes a virus can alter or hijack our genes, which eventually leads to cancer,” Dr. Smith says. “When we vaccinate against a known virus that can cause cancer, we have an opportunity to interrupt that process before it starts.” Vaccines aren’t “just for kids,” and flu and COVID-19 shots aren’t the only ones available to adults in their 20s, 30s and 40s. For this reason, oncologists urge adults 45 and under to ask about one vaccine in particular, as it could protect them from several cancers. 🩺 SIGN UP for Parade’s health newsletter with expert-approved tips, healthy eats, exercises, news & more to help you stay healthy & feel your best self 💊 Oncologists Are Begging Adults 45 and Under to Ask About This Vaccine Oncologists urge people 45 and under to get the HPV vaccine because it can protect you against six types of cancer: Cervical, oropharyngeal (throat), anal, vulvar, vaginal and penile. The HPV vaccine can stop “the underlying viral infection that causes” these cancers, says Dr. Ami Vaidya, MD , co-chief of the Division of Gynecologic Oncology at the Hackensack Meridian John Theurer Cancer Center. The FDA approved the first HPV vaccine in 2006, and it targeted four variants of human papillomavirus (HPV), a virus that commonly spreads through sexual contact. In 2014, the FDA approved the Gardasil 9 HPV vaccine , which doctors still use today. Dr. Vaidya says it targets nine high-risk viral strains of HPV. Doctors recommend the HPV vaccine to all children ages 11–12 (but children can begin getting the vaccination at age nine). It’s a two-dose series for ages 9–14. However, people can receive a three-dose series up to age 45. “The vaccine is made with the outer coating of the virus to teach your immune system to recognize the virus and create antibodies that can then destroy the virus if you are exposed to it in the future, before it causes an infection,” Dr. Smith says. “Since the vaccine does not contain any DNA from the virus, you cannot get infected with HPV from the vaccine.” Related: ‘I’m an Oncologist—This Is the First Symptom I’d Never Ignore in Someone Under 40′ Advertisement Why Do Oncologists Recommend the HPV Vaccine to People Ages 27-45? The recommended age for the HPV vaccine is 11-12 years, but people can receive their first dose at age 9. Doctors and medical organizations like the CDC continue to recommend the HPV vaccine for people ages 13-26 (the “catch-up” demographic). However, Dr. Vaidya encourages people to ask about the vaccine up to and including age 45, saying the vaccine remains “highly beneficial” for many people. It provides robust protection against any of the nine high-risk viral strains a person has not yet encountered,” Dr. Vaidya says. “This is especially crucial for individuals experiencing life transitions—such as re-entering the dating pool after a breakup or divorce—which introduce new opportunities for exposure.” She adds that natural HPV infections don’t always give you lasting immunity, so the vaccine offers a “much stronger antibody response” that can guard you against reinfection, lower your long-term health risks like throat cancer and protect future partners from transmission. Related: ‘I Was Diagnosed With Cancer at 16 and Again at 39—These Were the Very First Symptoms I Noticed’ Dr. Vaidya says there’s no approved HPV vaccine for people ages 46 and older because many people in this age group were already exposed to the virus during sexual activity. “Immunization can only prevent new infections, not treat or clear existing ones,” she says. Dr. Vaidya adds that HPV is a slow-acting virus and usually takes one to three decades of persistent infection to progress to cancer. “A new infection acquired later in life is much less likely to develop into cancer within a person’s natural lifespan,” she says. But if you’re 45 and under, Drs. Vaidya and Smith agree that it’s worth asking your doctor about the HPV vaccine. “Health experts recommend ‘shared clinical decision-making,’ meaning adults should consult with their doctor to determine if vaccination aligns with their current lifestyle and personal risk factors,” she says. Up Next: Related: The Lung Cancer Screening Oncologists Say Almost No One Eligible Gets (But Should) Sources: Dr. Ami Vaidya, MD, the co-chief of the Division of Gynecologic Oncology at the Hackensack Meridian John Theurer Cancer Center Dr. Gabrielle Smith, MD , a gynecologic oncologist with HonorHealth Survival Rates for Breast Cancer. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Dual Molecular Assays Show Strong Agreement for Cervical Cancer Screening in Cameroon by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dual Molecular Assays Show Strong Agreement for Cervical Cancer Screening in Cameroon Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers evaluating primary cervical cancer screening strategies in Cameroon have demonstrated high diagnostic concordance between two widely available commercial molecular platforms detecting high-risk oncogenic human papillomavirus. In a cross-sectional study analyzing endocervical swab samples from adult women, investigators compared the analytical performance of the Abbott RealTime High Risk human papillomavirus assay performed on the m2000rt instrument with the Sacace HPV Genotypes 14 Real-TM Quant assay executed on the QuantStudio 7 Flex platform. The findings, reported in Infectious Agents and Cancer, reveal a Cohen kappa coefficient of 0.800 between the systems, establishing that these multiplex molecular platforms can operate interoperably within resource-constrained national healthcare frameworks seeking to expand cervical screening access. Cervical cancer represents a severe public health burden in Cameroon, where model estimates indicate that approximately 2,770 women receive a cervical cancer diagnosis annually and 1,787 women die from the malignancy. Although the World Health Organization has established global elimination targets for 2030 that require screening 70 percent of adult women with high-performance molecular assays by age 35 and 45, Cameroon currently lacks a standardized national screening algorithm or systematic government screening program. Existing testing initiatives have largely remained sporadic, driven predominantly by civil society organizations and clinical research institutions. Expanding screening coverage has encountered structural hurdles due to the high capital expense of deploying dedicated molecular testing instruments across decentralized regional hospitals, prompting researchers to assess whether existing infrastructure can be repurposed. To address this diagnostic gap, investigators leveraged molecular laboratory instruments originally distributed across Cameroon for other public health priorities. While centralized reference facilities have maintained Abbott platforms for decades to support human immunodeficiency virus viral load quantification, decentralized regional treatment centres received open QuantStudio 7 Flex real-time polymerase chain reaction instruments during emergency laboratory expansions for SARS-CoV-2 testing. Because these multi-pathogen platforms remain underutilized following the acute phase of the coronavirus pandemic, establishing the analytical comparability of assays running on these distinct instruments provides an empirical pathway to scale decentralized cervical screening without requiring prohibitive procurement of new closed-system machinery. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding The study protocol recruited 364 adult female participants aged 18 years and older who presented for cervicovaginal screening between April and November 2023 at two major metropolitan tertiary healthcare facilities: the Gynaeco-Obstetric and Pediatric Hospital of Yaounde and the Gynaeco-Obstetric and Pediatric Hospital of Douala. Sample size determination utilized Cochran’s formula based on an anticipated national human papillomavirus prevalence of 20.9 percent reported in International Agency for Research on Cancer statistical registries, requiring a minimum enrollment threshold of 254 individuals. The participant cohort exhibited a median age of 41 years, with an interquartile range extending from 34 to 50 years, closely matching the target demographic recognized to carry higher vulnerability to invasive cervical malignancy. Specimen collection followed standardized operating protocols utilizing Abbott Cervi-Collect specimen collection devices, with swabs preserved in PreservCyt medium and stored in cryo-racks at minus 80 degrees Celsius before batch processing at the Chantal Biya International Reference Centre for research on HIV/AIDS prevention and care in Yaounde. For the Abbott assay, automated nucleic acid extraction was executed with 400-microliter input volumes on the m2000sp instrument, followed by real-time fluorescent probe amplification on the m2000rt system to detect genotypes 16 and 18 individually alongside a pooled detection channel covering twelve additional high-risk viral types. Comparative analysis with the Sacace assay extracted genomic material from 200-microliter samples using QIAamp DNA Mini kits prior to multiplex amplification identifying 14 specific high-risk genotypes individually. Discover more Donate to Research Find Conferences Health Initial diagnostic screening of the 364 enrolled participants revealed overall high-risk human papillomavirus positivity rates of 21.4 percent, representing 78 positive samples, using the Abbott platform, compared to 15.4 percent, or 56 positive samples, using the Sacace platform. Cross-tabulation demonstrated a positive concordance of 72 percent, with 56 samples concordantly positive across both platforms, and a negative concordance of 93 percent, reflecting 286 samples confirmed negative by both diagnostic systems. The observed statistical agreement yielded a Cohen kappa value of 0.800 with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.721 to 0.879, meeting the defined criteria for strong diagnostic agreement between independent multiplex diagnostic technologies. To resolve analytical discrepancies, investigators subjected all 22 discordant specimens—each testing positive by Abbott but negative by Sacace—to independent secondary arbitration using the Anyplex II HPV28 genotyping kit, which simultaneously identifies 19 high-risk and 9 low-risk types. Arbitration analysis confirmed the presence of high-risk viral sequences in 19 of the 22 discordant specimens, or 86.36 percent, while only three samples retained complete undetectability. Following arbitration, the verified cumulative prevalence of high-risk human papillomavirus infection in the studied cohort reached 20.6 percent, corresponding to 75 confirmed positive individuals. Authors noted that analytical discordance stemmed primarily from divergent analytical detection limits, as Sacace thresholds report viral loads around 1,000 genomic equivalents per 100,000 cells, whereas Abbott captures lower viral concentrations. Genotypic discrimination conducted across confirmed cases identified 12 circulating high-risk oncogenic types in the cohort, with genotypes 31 and 51 remaining completely undetected. Among positive isolates, human papillomavirus genotype 16 appeared most frequently, representing 18.8 percent of detected infections, followed closely by genotype 18 at 16.0 percent, genotype 39 at 16.0 percent, and genotype 58 at 13.0 percent. The prominent detection of genotypes 39 and 58 highlights localized genetic diversity that contrasts with historical surveys among female sex workers in Cameroon, where genotypes 51, 53, and 52 predominated, as well as cytological cohorts in Yaounde that observed higher relative frequencies of genotype 45 alongside types 16 and 18. A comparative health-economic analysis conducted by the investigators identified critical structural trade-offs between consumable costs and platform capital requirements. Reagent expenses alone favored the Abbott assay, which demonstrated an operating reagent cost of approximately 11.82 United States dollars per test, compared to 23.36 dollars per test for the Sacace assay, representing a 50.6 percent lower consumable cost per individual examination. However, deploying new proprietary Abbott instruments across peripheral healthcare centers requires substantial capital investments that regional budgets cannot support. Because public regional hospitals across Cameroon already possess functional QuantStudio 7 Flex instruments, utilizing these decentralized open systems allows health authorities to bypass capital procurement expenses, offsetting higher unit reagent costs through local multi-pathogen testing efficiency. Synthesizing their diagnostic and economic findings, the researchers proposed a standardized operational screening algorithm tailored for resource-limited settings. Under this strategic framework, reference laboratories equipped with existing Abbott systems continue high-throughput primary screening utilizing the assay’s superior analytical sensitivity and lower reagent expenses, while peripheral regional facilities utilize open QuantStudio instruments to deliver accessible frontline detection and comprehensive genotypic discrimination. The authors noted that a primary limitation of their evaluation involved comparing only two proprietary assay chemistries, emphasizing that future research should examine broader panels of commercial reagents to further refine interoperable screening protocols across sub-Saharan Africa. Detailed clinical examination and sociodemographic profiling of the study cohort offered broader insights into screening-seeking behavior among Cameroonian women. Beyond age distributions, clinical assessments revealed that 68.4 percent of participants, representing 249 women, presented with normal vaginal discharges and no demonstrable cervical inflammation. Mild cervical inflammation occurred in 15.4 percent (56 women), moderate inflammation was documented in another 15.4 percent (56 women), and only 0.8 percent (three women) presented with severe cervical inflammation. Educational attainment within the cohort was substantial, with 84.9 percent having completed at least secondary-level schooling. Regarding reproductive and behavioral history, 79.9 percent reported their sexual debut occurred before age 20, 62.1 percent were married, divorced, or widowed, and 59.1 percent recorded a history of two to six pregnancies. The authors observed that the high proportion of asymptomatic women presenting without inflammation demonstrates meaningful public awareness and voluntary participation in preventive screening despite the absence of an organized national program. Beyond aggregate positivity, concordance between the two test kits was further mapped across five distinct high-risk viral diagnostic categories. Among the 78 positive specimens detected by Abbott, eleven samples tested positive solely for genotype 16, six specimens were positive exclusively for genotype 18, two contained genotype 16 alongside other high-risk types, three carried genotype 18 with other types, and 56 fell into the pooled other high-risk category. Discrepancies in the detection of different or identical genotypes proved most prominent for HPV 18, occurring in six of nine discordant evaluations. Methodological controls maintained strict data integrity throughout the study, including ethical clearance from the Regional Ethics Committee and written assent from all participants. The researchers also contextualized their findings within broader international challenges in molecular cervical screening. According to global inventories, between 50 percent and 79 percent of more than 250 commercially available molecular assays lack peer-reviewed publications or sufficient evidence demonstrating their analytical performance quality. While other platforms present in Cameroon, including Cobas and GeneXpert systems, identify high-risk infections, they do not provide the detailed genotypic discrimination enabled by the QuantStudio platform. Establishing rigorous local interoperability between existing instruments therefore provides a verified foundation for standardized national screening guidelines. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Cervical Screening Study in Zimbabwe Evaluates Motivations and Preferences Among Women by November 20, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cervical Screening Study in Zimbabwe Evaluates Motivations and Preferences Among Women Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A health facility survey across three public-sector clinics in Zimbabwe has evaluated the motivations and hesitations regarding cervical cancer screening among women living with HIV, providing empirical evidence as the country transitions from visual inspection with acetic acid and cervicography to molecular human papillomavirus testing. Published in Infectious Agents and Cancer, the cross-sectional investigation revealed that while overall acceptance of annual visual screening was remarkably high among clinic attendees, women who declined visual examinations frequently cited physical discomfort during pelvic examinations and expressed strong interest in alternative HPV-based testing methods, including self-collection. Cervical cancer represents a severe public health burden in low- and middle-income countries, where persistent infections with high-risk human papillomaviruses cause the majority of disease cases. In Zimbabwe, cervical cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and the leading cause of cancer mortality among women, resulting in an estimated 3,000 diagnoses and 2,200 deaths each year. The intersection of this oncologic burden with high HIV prevalence further elevates risk, as women living with HIV are six times more likely to experience persistent HPV infections that advance to high-grade cervical lesions at younger ages than their HIV-negative peers. To address this dual burden, national cervical cancer control efforts supported by the Zimbabwe Technical Assistance, Training and Education Center for Health, known as Zim-TTECH, historically scaled up annual single-visit screen-and-treat protocols using visual inspection with acetic acid and cervicography, abbreviated as VIAC. In 2023 alone, these initiatives screened 100,117 women living with HIV across 360 public facilities in five provinces. However, aligned with updated 2021 World Health Organization recommendations, Zimbabwe revised its national screening guidelines in 2023 to adopt molecular HPV DNA testing every three to five years as the primary screening tool, reserving VIAC for triage to guide treatment eligibility. Discover more Research assistant services Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Cancer research funding To assess client readiness for this strategic transition, investigators administered a structured 31-item paper questionnaire between February and June 2023 to a convenience sample of 451 women living with HIV aged 18 to 49 years. The evaluation was conducted at three purposively selected public-sector facilities operated by the Ministry of Health and Child Care: Glenview Polyclinic, an urban outpatient facility in Harare; Guruve District Hospital, a rural referral facility in Mashonaland Central Province; and Tsholotsho District Hospital, serving rural communities in Matabeleland North Province. Questionnaires were administered in Shona or Ndebele by nurse interviewers who were distinct from the healthcare providers who offered or conducted the clinical examinations. Among the 451 participants who completed the assessment, 414 women, representing 91.8 percent of the cohort, accepted same-day VIAC screening, whereas 37 women, or 8.2 percent, declined the procedure. Participant demographics showed a median age of 40 years, with an interquartile range of 33 to 45 years. Most respondents demonstrated long-standing engagement with HIV care; 76.3 percent had known their HIV-positive status for five years or more, 74.5 percent had attended the participating clinic for at least five years, and 99.8 percent were receiving antiretroviral therapy. Furthermore, 73.4 percent of participants reached their respective health facilities by walking. Among the 414 women who accepted VIAC screening, 323 women, accounting for 78.0 percent, were presenting for re-screening, while 91 women, or 22.2 percent, were undergoing screening for the first time. The motivations driving uptake differed markedly based on prior screening history. Women presenting for repeat examinations primarily cited a desire to feel secure about their personal health, which accounted for 45.8 percent of responses, followed by compliance with annual screening recommendations at 39.6 percent, and encouragement from healthcare workers at 8.0 percent. Conversely, first-time screeners identified healthcare worker encouragement as their primary driver at 39.6 percent, followed by adherence to annual screening recommendations at 38.5 percent, and health reassurance at 17.6 percent. When questioned about their future screening preferences, the majority of women who accepted VIAC indicated a clear desire to continue with visual inspection rather than shift to molecular testing. Specifically, 70.3 percent of women attending re-screening and 89.0 percent of first-time screeners preferred continuing with VIAC. The authors observed that this preference likely reflected familiarity and existing trust in visual modalities, as most participants were introduced to the concepts of HPV testing and self-sampling for the first time during the questionnaire administration through a standardized explanatory script. Discover more Donate to Research Find Conferences health Health Cancer A distinct pattern emerged among the 37 women who declined VIAC screening. Despite 78.4 percent knowing their HIV status for at least five years and 73.0 percent having attended the same facility for five or more years, 75.7 percent of this group had never undergone cervical cancer screening, even though 43.2 percent had been offered screening more than once in the past. The dominant barrier to uptake was procedural apprehension: 54.1 percent cited fear of physical discomfort associated with the speculum-guided pelvic examination, 13.5 percent expressed worry regarding the potential screening result, and 10.8 percent cited perceived side effects of VIAC. Importantly, nearly half of the women who declined VIAC screening, representing 48.6 percent of the refusal group, indicated a preference for future HPV testing over visual inspection. Among the 18 hesitant women who favored HPV testing, preferences regarding specimen collection were distributed across multiple modalities: 21.6 percent favored provider-collected sampling, 16.2 percent preferred self-collection conducted at home, and 13.6 percent preferred self-collection performed at the health facility. Among the 93 women with prior screening experience who favored HPV testing, preference was evenly split between facility-based self-collection at 13.6 percent and provider-collected sampling at 13.9 percent. The study authors highlighted several operational considerations for health systems scaling up molecular testing within routine HIV services. Because existing clients exhibit strong loyalty to familiar VIAC protocols, programs must implement client-centered education that clarifies the clinical rationale and enhanced sensitivity of molecular HPV testing, as well as the safety of extended three-to-five-year screening intervals. Simultaneously, offering validated self-sampling options provides an actionable pathway to engage women who systematically avoid speculum examinations due to discomfort or modesty concerns, ensuring broader population coverage. Beyond core clinical history, the survey captured detailed social and demographic profiles across the three participating medical centers. Among all enrolled participants, 64.1 percent reported completing secondary education, and 66.3 percent were currently married. Religious affiliations were predominantly Christian at 44.3 percent, followed by Pentecostal at 24.4 percent and Apostolic at 19.7 percent. Facility representation included 164 women from Glenview Polyclinic, 163 from Tsholotsho District Hospital, and 124 from Guruve District Hospital. Among respondents with previous screening experience, 68.7 percent had undergone visual evaluation one to two years prior, 25.7 percent within the preceding twelve months, and 5.6 percent more than two years earlier. Study procedures adhered to protocols approved by the Medical Research Council of Zimbabwe and evaluated under United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention human research protection guidelines, with paper records digitized into CommCare and analyzed in R software. The investigation highlighted practical service delivery dynamics, particularly the physical and time burdens borne by clients. A substantial majority of respondents had existing employment commitments, traveled on foot, and required at least thirty minutes to arrive at health facilities. Although differentiated HIV service delivery models, such as multi-month dispensing of antiretroviral drugs and community clubs, reduce clinic transit burdens and preserve viral suppression, they concurrently diminish regular face-to-face contacts with clinic workers. In supported sites, healthcare staff currently utilize a manual, color-coded sticker mechanism on medical records to identify clients overdue for visual screening. However, this visual tracking approach risks missing women enrolled in multi-month dispensing who visit clinics infrequently. Consequently, investigators suggested implementing automated tracking and alert systems to reliably schedule molecular testing every three to five years while documenting screening declinations for personalized follow-up. Participant age patterns also underscored the necessity of sustained educational outreach across different life stages. First-time screening uptake and procedural refusals were both documented among women aged 41 to 49 years despite their prolonged retention in primary HIV care. Under updated national guidance, primary molecular testing is directed toward women living with HIV between the ages of 25 and 49 years. The researchers emphasized that older women must not be neglected during this transition, citing global guidance recommending at least one molecular test for unscreened women aged 50 to 65 years when clinical visualization of the cervix is limited. Additionally, cultural and community networks offer critical touchpoints for health communication. Because approximately one quarter of refusing participants belonged to the Apostolic faith, a tradition previously linked to spiritual healing preferences over clinical preventive care, tailored provider dialogue and collaborative outreach with faith leaders could help dispel reservations regarding cancer prevention. The authors noted several methodological considerations that temper the generalizability of their conclusions. The cross-sectional sample was drawn exclusively from three public facilities, meaning findings might not capture conditions across all healthcare environments in Zimbabwe. Additionally, because most participants learned about molecular screening solely through the introductory questionnaire script, their stated acceptance levels and collection preferences represent preliminary perspectives. Potential social desirability bias was managed by deploying interviewer nurses separate from clinical screening providers, though investigators could not calculate the median interval between antiretroviral treatment initiation and first screening because initiation dates were unrecorded. With HPV vaccination rates falling and screening lagging, our goal of becoming the first country to eliminate cervical cancer can no longer be assumed. Australia promised to be the first country to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035, something I’ve previously described as one of the more positive stories in women’s health. But that goal could be slipping away as HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccinations have fallen below 80 per cent for the first time, and to their lowest levels since the national program began in 2007. Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers that is almost entirely preventable. While an elimination goal once seemed like a dream, it is well within reach for Australia if we can maintain vaccination rates and cervical screening participation. But HPC coverage dropped to 77.1 per cent in 2025, and down to 69.6 per cent among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adolescents – down more than 15 points since 2020. Meanwhile, only three-quarters of eligible Australians are up to date with screening. The Cervical Cancer Elimination Progress report released today for World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day shows that the proportion of girls receiving a dose of HPV vaccine by age 15 fell from 80 per cent to 78.7 per cent, while coverage for boys also continued to decline, falling to 75.6 per cent The report notes that sustained vaccination coverage below 80 per cent is not sufficient for achieving elimination of the targeted HPV types in the longer term, and experts are calling for urgent action to reverse the trend. As Julia Brotherton (pictured above), lead author of the report, says, Australia’s made extraordinary progress in eliminating cancer, but this progress can’t be taken for granted. “Anyone aged 25 or under who has missed their HPV vaccination can catch up with a free single dose. I encourage young people and parents to speak with their GP, nurse or pharmacist,” says Brotherton, who is also Professor of Cancer Prevention at the University of Melbourne. Professor Lisa Whop, Associate Director of Research and Cervical Cancer Elimination Team Lead at Yardhura Walani, the Australian National University, also notes how quickly the hard-won gains can be lost, sharing concern for the decline in HPV vaccination among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adolescents. “We need sustained investment in culturally safe, community-led approaches, stronger partnerships with Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations and schools, and better pathways to reach young people who miss school-based vaccination,” she said. The vaccine protects against high-risk strains of HPV that lead to cancers of the cervix, vaina, vulva, penis, anus and back of the throat. It can also protect against non-cancer-causing HPV strains that are responsible for the vast majority of genital warts. The vaccine works best before a person is ever exposed through sexual contact, which is why it’s typically recommended it’s given to early adolescence. The World Health Organisation urged the globe to work together to eliminate cervical cancer in 2018, and it is an area of health that has shown that the eradication of a disease could be possible with leadership and sustained focus. The work that has been achieved – including moving recently to the availability of a self-collection method for screening, improving participation rates among under-screened populations – comes as a result of decades of support for an organised approach that is the cervical screening program. Australia’s National Strategy for the Elimination of Cervical Cancer was launched in November 2023, with the goal of elimination by 2035. Its modelling includes targets of 90 per cent vaccination coverage among eligible people, 70 per cent participation in five-yearly cervical screening, and 95 per cent of eligible people receiving optimal treatment for cervical precancer and cancer. But as Professor Marion Saville told me in 2021, equity in the program has always been the biggest challenge. Communities can’t be left behind in Australia’s race to be the first country to eliminate cervical cancer, especially Aboriginal women who are already two and a half to three times more likely to develop this cancer than other Australian women. Around 250 Australian women die from cervical cancer each year, according to Cancer Australia. Mortality rates dropped significantly in recent decades due to the immunisation and screening program, but the majority of individuals who do die of cervical cancer have either never participated in screening or are under-screened, according to the Australian Centre for Disease Control. All of this shows why cervical screening remains critical, even despite Australia’s successful HPV vaccination program – something I’ll admit I personally fell behind on until earlier this year, actually thinking the vaccination program had it sorted. So take this as a reminder to check if you’re overdue for screening, or to get that first vaccination dose for those 25 and under. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Bruceine D Induces Ferroptosis in Immortalized Ectocervical Epithelial Cells by November 19, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Bruceine D Induces Ferroptosis in Immortalized Ectocervical Epithelial Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A plant-derived compound called bruceine D significantly reduced the survival of human papillomavirus-immortalized cervical cells by triggering ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Researchers identified the quassinoid, isolated from Brucea javanica, as an active agent capable of impairing ectocervical cells expressing HPV16 E6 and E7 oncogenes in laboratory culture. Because persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus strains represents the primary underlying cause of cervical precancerous lesions and cervical cancer, evaluating compounds that trigger regulated cellular demise in affected tissues has become an area of active therapeutic investigation. To evaluate the biological effects of the natural compound, investigators conducted experiments on HPV16 E6/E7-immortalized ectocervical epithelial cells, designated as Ect1/E6E7. The team assessed cellular proliferation and health through multiple experimental assays, measuring cell viability, colony formation capacity, EdU incorporation, and cell-cycle progression. Across these assays, the treatment significantly inhibited cell proliferation and provoked cell-cycle arrest at the G0/G1 transition in a concentration-dependent manner, indicating that exposure prevented the cells from dividing normally. Subsequent laboratory tests demonstrated that the cellular death induced by bruceine D possessed the classical molecular hallmarks of ferroptosis. Following compound administration, the cervical cells showed a substantial increase in lipid peroxidation and elevated levels of malondialdehyde, a primary byproduct of lipid damage. In parallel, intracellular levels of the antioxidant glutathione were depleted, and mitochondrial function was severely disrupted, matching the metabolic imbalances typically observed when ferroptotic cascades are initiated. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Read Med Journals Study Anatomy Find Cancer Care The study also analyzed the expression of ferroptosis-related proteins to characterize the molecular cascades governed by the treatment. Exposure to bruceine D treatment downregulated GPX4 in the cultured cells. The functional contribution of this pathway was further validated through pharmacological rescue experiments, in which specific ferroptosis inhibitors partially reversed cell death, confirming that iron-dependent oxidative lethality contributed directly to the observed cytotoxicity. To uncover the regulatory networks acting alongside GPX4 downregulation, the researchers utilized network pharmacology analysis coupled with experimental validation. These integrated analyses implicated glutathione S-transferase P1, designated GSTP1, and mitogen-activated protein kinase 14, known as MAPK14, as central components in the cellular response to bruceine D. When the scientists applied pharmacological inhibitors targeting MAPK14, the ferroptotic responses were markedly attenuated, demonstrating that GSTP1 and MAPK14 signaling serves as an important regulatory pathway during compound exposure. Beyond single-agent administration, the researchers evaluated the impact of combining bruceine D with established small-molecule modulators of ferroptotic signaling. When administered alongside the known ferroptosis inducer erastin, the quassinoid exhibited synergistic antiproliferative effects, leading to an enhanced suppression of Ect1/E6E7 cell growth compared to individual treatments. The researchers noted that these preclinical findings warrant further experimental investigation into bruceine D and ferroptosis-targeted strategies in the context of HPV-associated cervical disease.
