Print HPV detection Chennai: Women in five Tamil Nadu districts will be offered kits to collect their own samples for a test that detects a virus, human papillomavirus, linked to cervical cancer.On Tuesday, world cervical cancer elimination day, state health department published a government order approving ₹8.7 crore to screen 1.24 lakh women for high-risk HPV in five districts. The order, signed by health secretary Darez Ahamed, said the programme would be extended to other districts in phases, subject to Union government approval.The kits will allow women to take a vaginal swab themselves at their homes, without an intimate examination by a doctor or nurse. Health centres will collect the samples and send them to a laboratory. The programme will cover women aged 35 in Dharmapuri, Villupuram, Tiruvannamalai, Perambalur and Ariyalur. They will be screened again at 45, said Dr J Jayashree, programme officer for cancer care at the National Health Mission, Tamil Nadu.Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in Tamil Nadu, despite being largely preventable through vaccination, regular screening and timely treatment. The state’s cancer registry says it continues to rank second in the state and first in some districts, even as its incidence has declined. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like What She Discovered About Her Everyday Walking ShoesHF Stride Undo The new programme aims to identify women with high-risk HPV infections and treat precancerous changes before they develop into cancer. “Self-collection could help reach women who are reluctant to visit a hospital or undergo an examination,” she said. Officials are identifying a vendor to carry out the laboratory tests. The test looks for the genetic material of high-risk types of HPV virus. “It checks for the virus, not a woman’s inherited cancer risk. A positive result means she carries the virus,” she said.Until now, Tamil Nadu has largely screened for cervical cancer by having a health worker examine the cervix, the lower part of the womb, after applying dilute acetic acid. The worker looks for changes that may signal abnormal cells. That method depends on the examiner’s skill and judgement, Dr Jayashree said. The HPV test is more sensitive and less dependent on visual interpretation.Women who test positive will need further checks to determine whether the infection has caused abnormal cell changes. Those found to have precancerous changes — cells that could become cancer if left untreated — will receive treatment. Women diagnosed with cancer will be referred for cancer care. “Most HPV infections clear on their own. But an infection that persists can cause changes in cervical cells and, over time, lead to cancer. The vaccination drive protects girls against HPV, while screening helps identify women who need further assessment and treatment, she said. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Six-Gene Panel Distinguishes HPV-Positive Cervical and Head and Neck Cancers by November 17, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Six-Gene Panel Distinguishes HPV-Positive Cervical and Head and Neck Cancers Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive investigation integrating bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses has identified 52 shared genes associated with human papillomavirus across cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. From this group of shared alterations, a machine learning-based feature selection strategy prioritised a six-gene panel consisting of CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, MCM2, KCNS1, EFNB3, and COL28A1. This prioritised panel consistently distinguished HPV-positive tumours from HPV-negative tumours in both malignancies, pointing to common molecular pathways driven by viral infection despite the different anatomical origins of the two cancers. Human papillomavirus is recognised as the primary cause of cervical cancer and is also an increasingly significant contributor to head and neck malignancies. Although cervical tumours and head and neck tumours emerge from distinct anatomical sites, their development shares an underlying viral aetiology. Despite this common causative factor, the molecular alterations associated with HPV across both disease types have remained incompletely understood, creating a need for comparative transcriptional studies to clarify the shared biological mechanisms underlying HPV-driven carcinogenesis. To detect transcriptional patterns common to both cancer types, the researchers designed an analytical framework combining differential expression analysis with weighted gene co-expression network analysis. They applied these computational techniques to compare HPV-positive tumours against normal tissues in both cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. This initial comparative step was structured to capture shared tumour-associated genes that deviate from baseline expression in healthy non-cancerous tissues across both sites. Discover more Find Cancer Care Cancers cancer cancers Cancer Because general tumour-related changes can overlap with virus-specific signatures, the research team implemented an additional filtering step to isolate alterations uniquely linked to human papillomavirus. The shared tumour-associated genes were refined by conducting direct comparisons between HPV-positive tumours and HPV-negative tumours within both cervical and head and neck cancer datasets. Candidate genes that emerged from this comparative refinement were subsequently processed through a machine learning-based feature selection strategy to identify the most robust predictive markers. The integrated differential expression and co-expression network pipeline initially yielded a total of 52 shared HPV-associated genes, from which the machine learning strategy prioritised six specific targets: CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, MCM2, KCNS1, EFNB3, and COL28A1. When evaluated across patient cohorts, this six-gene panel demonstrated a consistent ability to distinguish HPV-positive from HPV-negative tumours in both cervical cancer and head and neck cancer. Furthermore, the panel maintained similar expression patterns when tested against independent transcriptomic validation cohorts. To resolve how these candidate markers behave at cellular resolution, the authors examined single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from both tumour types. This analysis demonstrated that all six prioritised genes were predominantly expressed within epithelial cells. Within these epithelial cell populations, the directional expression changes corresponded to viral status: CDKN2A, CDKN2B-AS1, KCNS1, and MCM2 showed increased expression levels in HPV-positive samples, whereas EFNB3 and COL28A1 exhibited reduced expression in the presence of HPV infection. Functional annotation indicated that the six prioritised genes participate in key biological processes directly relevant to tumour progression. These biological functions include cell-cycle regulation, DNA replication, extracellular matrix organisation, and cell-to-cell communication. Additionally, the investigators examined how host gene expression corresponded with viral activity by correlating cellular transcript levels with HPV viral transcript levels, which revealed modest associations across the identified genes, most notably for CDKN2A and MCM2. Discover more Order DNA Kits Gene gene genes Check Symptoms In their conclusion, the authors stated that identifying these shared transcriptional alterations across cervical and head and neck cancers provides deeper insight into the molecular landscape of HPV-driven carcinogenesis. The authors emphasized that while these findings outline common transcriptional features linking two distinct malignancies, the identified gene panel primarily offers an empirical foundation for future studies focused on understanding HPV-associated tumour biology and discovering potential clinical biomarkers. In establishing the scientific rationale for the investigation, the authors noted that persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus represents the established, necessary cause of cervical cancer development, even though only a small proportion of HPV infections ultimately advance to high-grade cervical lesions or invasive malignancy. Clinical researchers have hypothesized that co-infections with genital mycoplasmas or classical sexually transmitted infections could potentially influence HPV persistence and disease progression, or alternatively impair the clinical accuracy of visual screening modalities by inducing local mucosal inflammation. Within Ethiopia, however, rigorous empirical evidence regarding the specific associations between these diverse sexually transmitted microbes, hrHPV infection status, histological cervical lesions, and visual inspection with acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine (VIA/VILI) has historically remained limited. To address this knowledge gap, the research team analyzed vaginal self-samples obtained from a study cohort of 885 Ethiopian women who participated in HPV-based cervical cancer screening protocols. The biological specimens were evaluated via real-time polymerase chain reaction (real-time PCR) assays designed to detect 14 high-risk HPV types, three classical sexually transmitted bacterial and protozoan pathogens—specifically Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis—and four species of genital mycoplasmas. Following initial molecular testing, clinical management pathways directed 156 women who tested positive for hrHPV to undergo visual inspection examinations using acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine, while 116 women subsequently underwent histological tissue examinations to establish definitive diagnostic classifications. Discover more Find Cancer Care See an OB-GYN Find Skin Care Book a Checkup Check Symptoms The authors employed rigorous analytical approaches to evaluate the collected epidemiological and molecular data, summarizing categorical variables through descriptive frequencies and percentages. Bivariate associations between the identified microbial detections and designated outcome variables were examined using chi-square tests alongside logistic regression models. The molecular analysis established that 568 participants, representing 64.2 percent of the study population (95 percent confidence interval: 61 to 67 percent), tested positive for at least one sexually transmitted microbe. Classical sexually transmitted infections were present in a relatively small subset of participants, yielding an overall prevalence of 4.3 percent (95 percent confidence interval: 3.1 to 5.8 percent). By contrast, genital mycoplasmas were widely distributed across the screening cohort, being identified in 64 percent of the women (95 percent confidence interval: 60.7 to 67.1 percent). Among the various mycoplasma species detected by real-time PCR, Ureaplasma parvum was documented as the most frequently identified organism, while approximately one out of every five women in the broader cohort was diagnosed with an hrHPV infection. Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that the detection of high-risk HPV was significantly associated with several distinct microbial detections and systemic infections. High-risk HPV positivity was statistically associated with the presence of genital mycoplasma detection (adjusted odds ratio = 1.7, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.3 to 2.3, p = 0.001), Chlamydia trachomatis infection (adjusted odds ratio = 5.4, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.4 to 21, p = 0.014), and Mycoplasma hominis detection (adjusted odds ratio = 2.0, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.4 to 3.0, p = 0.001). Furthermore, high-risk HPV was strongly associated with concurrent human immunodeficiency virus infection, which demonstrated an adjusted odds ratio of 3.2 (95 percent confidence interval: 1.8 to 5.5, p < 0.001). When evaluating tissue outcomes, histological examination revealed that cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) lesions were strongly associated with both high-risk HPV infection (adjusted odds ratio = 6.77, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.2 to 75.4, p = 0.03) and HIV infection (adjusted odds ratio = 8.92, 95 percent confidence interval: 1.5 to 72.2, p = 0.02). In contrast, neither the presence of classical sexually transmitted infections nor the detection of genital mycoplasmas showed a statistically significant association with CIN2+ cervical lesions or with the clinical outcomes of visual inspection using acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine. records.content: Province adopts HPV testing as primary cervical cancer screening tool Officials say the test can detect high‐risk infections before abnormal cell changes occur, allowing for earlier intervention The provincial government is transitioning to the human papillomavirus (HPV) test from the Pap test as the main form of cervical cancer screening in hopes of progressing cervical cancer prevention. HPV testing can detect the virus responsible for cervical cancer before abnormal cellular changes. This allows for earlier identification of people at risk and supports timely follow-up and intervention. "The research is clear; early detection of cancer can help save lives. By transitioning to HPV testing, we are improving our ability to identify individuals at risk of cervical cancer earlier, which is essential for prevention," said Health Minister John Dornan. "This change ensures that New Brunswickers have access to the most accurate, efficient and effective screening available." The move aligns with international and federal efforts to eliminate cervical cancer, including Canada's 2040 elimination goal. The work is in collaboration with all provinces and territories, which are at various stages of transitioning to HPV testing. "Switching to HPV testing represents a vital step forward in the fight against cervical cancer," said Dr. Eshwar Kumar, medical officer at the New Brunswick Cancer Network. "This approach allows us to pinpoint high-risk individuals earlier and implement the preventative care needed to save lives, giving New Brunswickers the best chance for long-term health." Health officials encourage New Brunswickers to maintain routine screening through their primary care provider. HPV testing is recommended every five years for women, trans men and gender-diverse people aged 25 to 69 who have a cervix and have ever been sexually active. People should speak with their provider about their personal screening needs. "Preventing cancer before it starts is one of the most powerful ways to save lives," said Andrea Seale, CEO of the Canadian Cancer Society. "We applaud New Brunswick for making HPV testing its primary cervical cancer screening method. This reflects the kind of action needed to deliver on Canada's commitment, reaffirmed through the G7, to eliminate cervical cancer, and is meaningful progress for New Brunswickers." A positive HPV test doesn't mean someone has cervical cancer; additional testing or follow-up may be recommended, depending on the results. More information about accessing cervical cancer screening is available on the government's website. She joined Britannica in 2006 and... Kara Rogers Fact-checked by Britannica Editors Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors oversee subject areas in which they have extensive knowledge, whether from years of experience gained by working on that content or via study for an advanced degree.... Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Pap smear, medical screening procedure used to detect precancerous and cancerous changes in the cells of the cervix. Developed in the 1940s by physician George Papanicolaou, the test involves collecting cells from the cervical surface during a pelvic examination and then investigating them microscopically for abnormalities. A Pap smear typically entails the collection of two specimens for laboratory staining and examination, one consisting of vaginal secretions from the ectocervix and the other of scrapings from the surface of the endocervical canal, where cancerous growth frequently originates. In practice, these cells may be collected together in one sample, such as when using a broom-type device for liquid-based cytology, or they may be collected separately, such as with a spatula for the ectocervix and a brush for the endocervical canal, and then combined in a single specimen vial or slide. The Pap smear may reveal malignant cells not only from the cervix but also from the endometrium (the mucous coat of the uterus) and the ovaries. The development of other cervical cancer screening methods, particularly human papillomavirus (HPV) testing and liquid-based cytology, has reshaped the role of the Pap smear in clinical practice. HPV testing, which directly detects the virus responsible for most cervical cancers, is more sensitive than cytology alone and in many regions of the world has been adopted as a primary screening tool or in combination with Pap smears (co-testing). Liquid-based cytology, introduced in the 1990s, improved sample quality and allowed concurrent HPV testing from the same specimen, increasing diagnostic efficiency. As a result, Pap smears are now performed less frequently, often at longer intervals (every 3–5 years rather than annually or biennially), and in some regions they are being replaced altogether by HPV-based screening. Despite these changes, the Pap smear remains an important tool worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings where HPV testing may be less accessible, and continues to be credited with dramatically reducing cervical cancer incidence and mortality since its introduction. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Honeycomb Ultrasound Patterns May Signal HPV-Independent Cervical Adenocarcinoma in Case Series by November 15, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Honeycomb Ultrasound Patterns May Signal HPV-Independent Cervical Adenocarcinoma in Case Series Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a retrospective case series analyzing patients who underwent surgery between August 2017 and September 2024, researchers have documented the clinical presentation and preoperative imaging patterns associated with gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma. Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma, commonly designated as G-EAC, is recognized as a distinct human papillomavirus-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma. To address these ongoing diagnostic difficulties, investigators reviewed records from thirteen patients with histopathologically confirmed disease at their medical center to characterize key clinical and sonographic manifestations and establish hypothesis-generating observations for subsequent clinical research. The investigated patient cohort consisted of thirteen parous women ranging from 39 to 76 years of age, with an overall mean age of 53.4 years across the series. An evaluation of presenting symptoms revealed that vaginal discharge was the most frequent complaint leading to evaluation, documented in eight of the thirteen patients, representing 61.5 percent of the cases. Irregular vaginal bleeding was identified as the second most common presenting symptom, reported in four of the thirteen women, or 30.8 percent. One patient, accounting for 7.7 percent of the cohort, presented with postcoital bleeding. Standard preoperative screening techniques demonstrated low diagnostic yields among the evaluated patients, underscoring the diagnostic hurdles typical of this human papillomavirus-independent malignancy. High-risk human papillomavirus testing returned negative findings in eleven of the thirteen individuals, or 84.6 percent. Cytological evaluation through ThinPrep cytologic testing, or TCT, similarly failed to identify malignant changes in the vast majority of cases, returning completely negative results in twelve of the thirteen women, or 92.3 percent. Discover more Find Cancer Care Donate to Research Read Med Journals Find Conferences Find an OBGYN Diagnostic limitations persisted when patients underwent colposcopic examination and directed tissue sampling prior to definitive surgical intervention. Among the eleven individuals in the cohort who underwent colposcopy accompanied by cervical biopsy, histopathological examination yielded negative results in eight of the eleven patients, or 72.7 percent. In two of the eleven biopsied individuals, representing 18.2 percent, the histopathological analysis identified mild glandular atypia. Definite neoplastic evidence was exceedingly rare during initial biopsy sampling, with rare adenocarcinoma cells identified in only one of the eleven patients, representing 9.1 percent of those who underwent the procedure. Ultrasound assessments raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in nine of the thirteen patients, or 69.2 percent. In contrast, sonographic findings were interpreted as suggestive of benign cervical cystic lesions in two of the thirteen patients, representing 15.4 percent, while findings were considered unremarkable in the remaining two patients, also accounting for 15.4 percent. Specific sonographic features were frequently observed across the cohort, including a characteristic honeycomb sonographic pattern identified in seven of the thirteen patients, or 53.8 percent. In addition, marked intralesional blood flow designated as Adler grade III abundant vascularity was detected in nine of the thirteen patients, representing 69.2 percent of the evaluated group. The study authors, affiliated with the Hunan Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital in Changsha, China, concluded that gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma may come to clinical attention through a combination of presenting symptoms and sonographic findings that collectively raise diagnostic suspicion. The researchers emphasized, however, that these findings remain strictly descriptive observations derived from a single-center retrospective series of thirteen patients, highlighting that larger, adequately controlled clinical studies are required to validate the diagnostic utility of these sonographic and clinical characteristics. MD 微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 (来源:德馨顺城) 宫颈癌,是严重威胁全球女性生命健康的恶性肿瘤,也是目前人类唯一可以通过疫苗预防的癌症。大量医学研究证实,几乎所有宫颈癌的发生,都与高危型人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)的持续感染密切相关。而接种HPV疫苗,是预防HPV感染、阻断宫颈癌发病链条,最经济、高效、科学的核心手段,是守护女性一生生殖健康的第一道坚固防线。 读懂HPV:无处不在的健康隐患 HPV病毒是一种极为常见的生殖道病毒,传播途径广泛,主要通过密切接触传播,有性生活的人群一生中感染HPV的概率高达80%以上。多数人感染后可自行清除病毒,但少数人会出现持续高危型感染,长期刺激宫颈细胞,逐步引发病变,最终发展为宫颈癌。 我国女性HPV感染存在两个高峰阶段,分别为17-24岁青年时期和40-44岁中年时期,覆盖女性青春、育龄、中年等关键人生阶段,隐蔽性强、危害持久。宫颈癌发病不可逆,且逐年呈现年轻化趋势,提前预防、主动防护,远比后期治疗更为重要。 黄金接种期:越早接种,保护力越强 世界卫生组织(WHO)明确推荐:9-14岁是接种HPV疫苗的黄金年龄。 这个阶段的青少年女孩,免疫系统发育完善,在尚未暴露于HPV病毒风险前接种,身体可产生远超成年人的抗体水平,抗体浓度是15岁以上人群的2倍以上,且保护时效更长久、防护效果更稳定,能最大程度规避后续病毒感染风险,实现最优预防效果。 很多人存在误区,认为“年纪小无需接种”“没有症状不用预防”。实则恰恰相反,HPV预防的核心关键,就是在病毒感染前建立免疫屏障。越早完成接种,越早获得专属保护,为终身生殖健康保驾护航。 多款疫苗适配全人群,按需选择无需焦虑 目前国内正规上市的HPV疫苗,分为二价、四价、九价三类,价数代表可预防的HPV病毒亚型种类,适配不同年龄、不同需求的女性,覆盖全面、各有优势。目前,我市主要有二价和九价2类HPV疫苗: 1.二价HPV疫苗:核心防护16、18型两种最高危病毒,这两种亚型诱发了全球70%以上的宫颈癌。适配9-45岁女性,性价比高、货源充足,是基础预防的优选,目前已纳入国家免疫规划。 2.九价HPV疫苗:覆盖9种高危及低危HPV亚型,可预防90%以上的宫颈癌及相关生殖道疾病,防护范围最广,适配9-45岁人群。 国家惠民政策落地,守护青少年健康 为全面降低我国女性宫颈癌发病率,国家已正式将13周岁适龄女孩免费接种二价HPV疫苗纳入国家免疫规划。 免费接种核心政策 •接种人群:2011年11月10日后出生、年满13周岁的适龄女孩 •接种剂次:全程2剂次,两剂间隔6个月,最长不超过1年 •接种地点:社区卫生服务中心、乡镇卫生院 这项普惠民生的健康政策,为青少年女孩免费搭建健康屏障,从源头降低下一代宫颈癌发病风险,是国家送给适龄女孩最珍贵的“健康礼”。免疫规划既是公民权利,也是公民义务,监护人应依法保证适龄儿童按时接种免疫规划疫苗。 破除常见误区,科学理性接种 1.误区1:接种疫苗就不会得宫颈癌 真相:HPV疫苗可预防绝大多数宫颈癌,但无法覆盖所有致病亚型,也不能替代日常筛查。疫苗接种+定期宫颈筛查,才是完整的防癌保障。 2.误区2:已有性生活、年纪大就不用接种 真相:无论是否有性生活、是否已婚、年龄大小,只要在接种年龄段,未感染对应高危亚型病毒,接种后均可获得有效保护,大龄女性依然有接种价值。 3.误区3:HPV疫苗只保护女性 真相:HPV病毒同样会引发男性尖锐湿疣、肛门癌等疾病,男性接种也可实现自我防护,同时减少病毒交叉传播,守护家人健康。 为爱接种,守护无恙 健康,是人生最珍贵的底色,也是陪伴一生的财富。宫颈癌可防可控,无需谈“癌”色变,主动接种HPV疫苗、定期做好健康筛查、树立健康防护意识,就能有效规避疾病风险。 无论是正值青春的少女,还是守护家庭的女性,都请重视生殖健康,把握黄金接种时机。积极接种HPV疫苗,主动筑牢免疫屏障,远离疾病困扰,拥抱自在健康人生! 温馨提示:所有HPV疫苗请通过正规接种单位接种,杜绝非正规渠道,保障接种安全。 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP 新浪财经声明:此消息系转载自合作媒体,新浪财经登载此文出于传递更多信息之目的,文章内容仅供参考,不构成投资建议。 一是今天大盘量能是放大的。不管是下跌还是上涨,只要大盘放量,就是好事情,本轮大盘见底应该是放量见底,这个观点,我们以前提示过很多次了。二是跌得最狠的那一批,先不跟了。上午大盘反弹首先拉升的是微盘股,严格说,本轮跌幅最大的就是微盘股,微盘股率先反弹,说明先跌的个股已经开始抵抗下跌了。三是豹子底来了。上证今天最低是3500.88点,创业板最低是2222.77点,这是标准的豹子底!现在就看能不能成立了!只要能够守住三天,这里出现一波反弹的概率还是很大的。互联网金融板块今天出现了一波拉升,本轮护盘主要护盘的是银行,但银行板块已经涨到天上去了,现在要寻求能够接力,而且还能带动人气的板块,只剩两个:一个是跟金融相关的互金、券商、保险,另外一个就是科技硬件。科技股跟外部联动较大,外围科技股连续大跌,想A股市场科技股单边大涨,这是不现实的,所以,现在只能拉升跟银行相关的金融股,但热点还是没有扩散到券商,券商如果启动,大盘反弹就有望展开。现在大盘在3000点以上的缺口都回补了,就剩下向下的缺口,按照A股逢缺必补的原则,首先应该是要向上回补最近的一个周线缺口3623点附近。愿接下来的行情,少一点惊吓,多一点像样的反弹。大家周末多陪陪老婆吧,这周都亏惨了。
